itineraries.title: Varanger in 4 Days: Kirkenes, Vardø, and Hamningberg
itineraries.subtitle: Over 4 days, follow the Varangerfjord from Kirkenes to Vardø, then take the summer road to Hamningberg.
itineraries.notes: The road to Hamningberg is closed in winter, and boats to Hornøya run roughly from mid-March through late August: aim for June or July. On the last day, allow about 3 hours 30 minutes to drive from Vardø to Kirkenes Airport.
itineraries.climate: Aim for June and July: in Vardø, average highs rise from 9 °C in June to 12 °C in July, and the sun does not set from May 16 to July 29. Bring a windbreaker, a warm hat, and rain gear, as the weather changes quickly and sea fog can roll in suddenly, even in summer. Avoid winter: the road to Hamningberg is closed, and storms are severe.
specialties: Histoire de la Seconde Guerre mondiale

visits.text: The temperature is around 0 °C inside Andersgrotta, the air-raid shelter dug beneath central Kirkenes in 1941. During World War II, the German army had a major base here: the town was bombed more than 300 times. The shelter could protect about 2,500 residents. The guided tour in English lasts 30 minutes, including a 10-minute film. It also takes in the statue of a Red Army soldier, erected in 1951 just above the shelter. Tours leave daily at 12:30 p.m. from the entrance, with prices starting at 350 NOK. The tour is not recommended for children under 12.

On October 25, 1944, when the Red Army liberated Kirkenes, only 13 houses were still standing. Grenselandmuseet, the borderland museum, tells the story of the war and life in the town before and after it. It also covers the Sydvaranger company’s iron mines and the culture of the Sámi, the Indigenous people of northern Scandinavia. A Soviet Ilyushin fighter plane is displayed in the war gallery. The museum is 1 km from the center. From June 20 to August 20, it is open from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m.

activities.text: Norwegians sometimes call it “Stalin’s crab.” The red king crab, native to the Pacific, was released by the Soviet Union into the Murmansk fjord in the 1960s. It then spread west into Norway, where it was first spotted as early as 1977. Its leg span can reach 1.8 m. On a king crab safari from Kirkenes, a fast inflatable boat takes you out onto the fjord, followed by a crab meal, usually one crab for two people. Allow 3 hours and about 2,500 NOK per adult, with warm clothing provided.

practical_info.tip: Summer trips depart from Kirkenes harbor from May to mid-September, for ages 7 and up. Book ahead.

visits.text: Várjjat Sámi Musea, the Varanger Sámi museum, occupies a building in Varangerbotn dating from 1994 and inspired by traditional Sámi houses. Its main exhibition focuses on the coastal Sámi, who made their living from fishing, reindeer herding, and raising farm animals. It reaches back to the Stone Age. It also presents ancient Sámi beliefs. The museum maintains the Mortensnes site, your next stop: visit here first to better understand it. Near the museum, a shelter displays a map of Varangerhalvøya National Park.

to_next_leg.road_type: Varanger National Scenic Route (E75)

visits.text: Modest, yet a survivor: the wooden church in Nesseby escaped the fires at the end of the war. As it retreated, the German army burned most buildings in Finnmark, and this church is one of the few older structures still standing. It was consecrated in 1858. Its prayer books are written in Northern Sámi. The church serves as a stopping point on the Varanger National Scenic Route, facing the fjord: a 30-minute break is enough.

11,000 years ago, the sea reached 70 m higher than it does today on the slope at Ceavccageađge, the Mortensnes cultural heritage site. Since the end of the Ice Age, the land, freed from the weight of the ice, has been slowly rising. This is why the oldest traces of settlement, dating back about 9,000 years, now lie 60 m above the water. The trails also lead to nearly 300 Sámi graves and a standing stone surrounded by 13 stone circles, an ancient offering site. Allow at least 1 hour for an easy walk.

to_next_leg.road_type: E75 along the Varangerfjord

visits.text: In Kven, the language of the descendants of Finnish immigrants, Vadsø is called Vesisaari. Innvandrermonumentet, the immigrant monument, honors the families who came from Finland and northern Sweden in the 19th century to escape famine. Sculptor Ensio Seppänen depicted an old man with a spade, his daughter carrying a child, and, behind them, her husband, a Norwegian fisherman. The kings of Norway and Sweden and Finnish President Kekkonen attended the unveiling on June 18, 1977. Walk around it: the anchor at the back symbolizes these families putting down roots here.

Vadsø’s most evocative museum is a former merchant’s house: Esbensengården, the Esbensen estate. It is part of Vadsø museum, also called Ruija kvenmuseum, the Kven museum. Here you can see a 19th-century merchant’s warehouses and the comforts his family enjoyed. The museum also tells the story of the Kvens’ arrival and the town’s history of fishing, farming, and trade. The museum houses open seasonally or on request: check opening hours with the Varanger Museum before visiting.

Tuomainengården, the Tuomainen farm, shows how a Kven family lived in Vadsø. Around the courtyard stand the house, barn, stable, forge, bakehouse—the room containing the bread oven—and sauna. The buildings illustrate local construction methods. A café operates here regularly, near the old bread oven. Like Esbensengården, the farm opens seasonally or on request: ask the museum for dates.

In 1926, the airship Norge moored at Luftskipsmasta, the mooring mast on the island of Vadsøya, before flying over the North Pole. On board were Roald Amundsen and the Italian Umberto Nobile. Nobile returned here in 1928 with another airship, the Italia. This is the only mast of its kind on the European mainland. It stands in Vadsøya Cultural Park, 500 m from the center via a bridge. A flat 1.8 km trail passes the remains of a medieval fishing village and German bunkers.

Gray concrete and straight lines: Vadsø Church, Vadsø kirke, looks unlike the wooden churches elsewhere on this trip. It was consecrated on March 30, 1958, and designed by architect Magnus Poulsson. It replaces the previous church, burned by the retreating German army on the night of October 28–29, 1944. It can accommodate about 480 people. If the door is open, take a look inside.

If you visit in summer, step inside Kjeldsenbruket, the former fish processing plant beside the dock in Ekkerøy. It is one of the few plants of its kind in Finnmark to have survived World War II. In the fall of 1944, the Soviet army advanced so quickly that German soldiers had no time to burn the village. You can still see the dock, grocery store, and cooker used to extract cod liver oil. The café and exhibitions open only in summer.

activities.text: The cries of black-legged kittiwakes drown out the wind at the foot of Flåget, the cliff in Ekkerøy Nature Reserve. Tens of thousands of these small, black-legged gulls nest here. This may be Norway’s most easily accessible seabird cliff. The 6.1 km loop circles Ekkerøy, a former island connected to the mainland by an isthmus, a narrow strip of land. At the top, you pass Gerda and Paula, two German gun emplacements that guarded the entrance to the fjord. Allow 2 hours for the walk.

practical_info.tip: Just before the dock in Ekkerøy, turn left and head uphill to the parking lot before the cliff. The kittiwakes return as early as March.

activities.text: Next, turn off the E75 toward Komagvær, farther east, and follow 7 km of unpaved road to Komagdalen, the valley of the Komagelva River. From Ekkerøy, plan on a round trip by car within the day, including the unpaved section. The parking lot marks the boundary of Varangerhalvøya National Park, established in 2006. The park covers 1,804 km², mostly tundra, an almost treeless landscape of plateaus, boulders, and peat bogs. A bird trail starts at the parking lot, with information panels about species such as the long-tailed jaeger, a characteristic bird of the park. The unpaved road is rough: drive slowly, preferably in a vehicle with high ground clearance.

practical_info.tip: Routes in the national park are not marked: bring a map and compass if you go beyond the bird trail. Dogs must be leashed from April 1 to August 20.

to_next_leg.road_type: E75, then 7 km round trip on an unpaved road toward Komagdalen

visits.text: The most powerful place on the trip is a long wooden corridor: Steilneset minnested, the memorial to the Vardø witch trials. From 1600 to 1692, 91 people from Finnmark, both Norwegians and Sámi, were sentenced to death for witchcraft. Many were burned on this very spot. Swiss architect Peter Zumthor incorporated 91 small windows into the corridor. Each is lit by a light bulb and paired with a plaque recounting one victim’s trial. In the neighboring glass pavilion, Louise Bourgeois installed a chair with a flame rising from it, surrounded by mirrors. Free access, day and night.

Vardøhus festning, Vardø’s fortress, forms an eight-pointed star. It was built from 1734 to 1738 on the site of an earlier fort erected around 1300. It is described as the world’s northernmost fortress. When the sun returns after the polar night, the winter period when it does not rise, the fortress fires two cannon shots, and Vardø’s schoolchildren get the rest of the day off. Look for the Kongestokken, an oak log into which Norwegian kings have carved their names. Free admission from 10 a.m. to 9 p.m. in summer.

Finnmark’s oldest museum is Vardø museum, which opened in 1894 as a natural history museum. Today it occupies Gammelskolen, the town’s former school. It tells the story of trade with the Pomors, Russian merchants from the White Sea who came every summer to buy fish and sell wheat and timber. This trade helped Vardø gain town status in 1789. The museum also covers fishing, the witch trials, and the partisans, the resistance fighters of World War II. Check opening hours with Varanger Museum, which oversees it.

activities.text: Ask the tourist office for a map of the murals in Vardø, Norway’s easternmost town. In 2012, the Komafest festival invited artists from around the world, including Portugal’s Vhils and Belgium’s Roa, to paint dozens of buildings, many of them vacant. The town had lost about half its population between the 1960s and the 2000s. The name comes from the Norwegian word koma, meaning coma: the idea was to wake up sleeping houses. As you arrive, note the Vardø Tunnel, which descends to 88 m below sea level over its 2.9 km length.

practical_info.tip: The mural map is available free at the tourist office by the harbor. You can explore the town center on foot.

to_next_leg.road_type: Narrow, winding road, closed in winter

visits.text: Abandoned, but not in ruins: Hamningberg is one of the few villages in Finnmark that the German army did not burn during its retreat in late 1944. About 65 old buildings are still standing: houses, boathouses, and warehouses. The fishermen sold their catch to the Pomors, Russian merchants. Many of the log houses were actually built in Russia and then reassembled here. In 1940, 700 people lived here. The village emptied out in the 1960s because its harbor offered too little shelter for modern boats. Walk past the wooden chapel built in 1949, which is protected as a historic landmark.

In May and early summer, Hamningberg’s birdwatching shelter lets you watch the sea out of the wind. It was designed by the architecture firm Biotope. Seabirds pass offshore. You can sometimes spot porpoises and minke whales, a species of whale, and, more rarely, orcas. To the west, the cliff of Syltefjordstauran is home to a large colony of northern gannets, large seabirds. Bring binoculars and a warm layer: it is easy to spend an hour standing still.

activities.text: You follow the final stretch of the Varanger National Scenic Route, which runs 160 km from Varangerbotn. After Vardø, the road to Hamningberg becomes narrow and winding. Along the coast, the weathered rocks often evoke a lunar landscape. Near Persfjorden, waves and frost have sculpted rocky spires that resemble trolls. Some of these rocks are more than 500 million years old. Stop at roadside pullouts for photos, and watch for reindeer.

practical_info.tip: The road is closed in winter; in 2026, it reopened on April 29. There is no gas station or store in Hamningberg: fill up and pick up a picnic in Vardø.

activities.text: If the weather is clear, climb Hardbaken, the hill that shelters Hamningberg from the north wind. A path leads from the village to the remains of a German coastal fort from World War II. From the top, the view takes in the Barents Sea and the rugged coastline. Look for snow buntings, small birds often seen on these heights. The paths are not maintained: follow the existing tracks, as the ground is slippery when wet.

practical_info.tip: The path starts in the village. Hiking shoes are recommended.

to_next_leg.road_type: Return to Vardø, then a 10-minute boat ride

visits.text: Hornøya is the easternmost point of mainland Norway, meaning Norway excluding the Svalbard archipelago. The island is even farther east than Istanbul. Vardø Lighthouse stands at its highest point, 65 m above the sea. Allow 15 minutes to walk there from the dock. From the top, the view extends over the Barents Sea and the bird colony. The neighboring island of Reinøya is closed to the public: just look at it from the path.

activities.text: Board a boat at Vardø’s harbor, behind the tourist office, for the 10-minute crossing to Hornøya, a seabird nature reserve. Atlantic puffins, black-legged kittiwakes, common murres, razorbills, and European shags nest on the cliff. You will also see thick-billed murres. A marked path passes very close to the nests: stay on it. Allow about 2 hours on the island.

practical_info.tip: Same-day tickets are available at Vardø’s tourist office: 630 NOK per adult in 2025 and 2026. Boats run from mid-March to late July or early August, with cancellations in rough weather: leave a half-day buffer.

to_next_leg.road_type: 10-minute boat ride, then the E75 along the fjord

activities.text: If your flight leaves Kirkenes in the early afternoon, leave Vardø early: allow about 3 hours 30 minutes to drive to Kirkenes, retracing your route along the Varangerfjord. Kirkenes Høybuktmoen Airport is about 5 km from town. Allow extra time, as reindeer often cross the road. Return your rental car at the airport.

practical_info.tip: Fill up in Vardø before leaving.

seo.h1_title: Varanger in 4 Days: Kirkenes, Vardø, and Hamningberg
seo.intro_paragraph: This 4-day road trip starts in Kirkenes and follows the Varangerfjord to Vadsø, Ekkerøy, and Vardø, in Norway’s far northeast. Along the way, you visit the Sámi museum in Varangerbotn, the prehistoric site of Mortensnes, and the gull cliff at Ekkerøy. From Vardø, you head up to the village of Hamningberg along a road open only in summer, then take a boat across to Hornøya, the island of puffins.
seo.seo_hook: Kirkenes’ air-raid shelter, Hornøya’s puffins, Vardø’s witches’ memorial, and the village of Hamningberg: Varanger in 4 days in summer.

itineraries.title: Norway’s Mountains in 5 Days: Lillehammer and Jotunheimen
itineraries.subtitle: In 5 days, travel up from Lillehammer to Lom, cross Sognefjellet Pass, and hike the Besseggen ridge.
itineraries.notes: The Gjende boat runs only from early June through September, and the Sognefjellet and Valdresflye roads close every winter: plan this trip between mid-June and mid-September. Book the boat for Besseggen and your overnight stay at Gjendesheim early, as both are in high demand in July and August.
itineraries.climate: Visit from late June to early September: in July, expect afternoon temperatures of around 22 °C in Lillehammer but barely 11 °C at Sognefjellet Pass, so pack a warm jacket. Avoid November through May, when the Gjende boat does not run and snow can close the high mountain roads. With around 320 mm of rain a year, Lom is one of the driest places in Norway.

activities.text: Pick up your rental car at Oslo Gardermoen Airport, about 47 km north of downtown Oslo. This route skips the capital and heads straight for the mountains. Lillehammer is 145 km north along the E6, a drive of less than 2 hours. If you land in the afternoon, save Maihaugen for the following morning: in summer, the museum generally opens at 10 a.m.

practical_info.tip: Car rental companies are located at the airport.

to_next_leg.road_type: E6 northbound

visits.text: The best starting point for understanding the Gudbrandsdal Valley is Maihaugen, Lillehammer’s large open-air museum. Dentist Anders Sandvig began collecting old houses from the valley in 1887. The museum opened at this site in 1904. Today, it has around 200 buildings. Among them, Garmo Church dates from the early 13th century. It is a stave church: its timber frame rests on large vertical posts. Allow 2 hours 30 minutes. In peak season, an adult ticket costs 235 NOK.

The Norwegian Olympic Museum (Norges olympiske museum) has been housed at Maihaugen since 2016. It tells the story of the Games from antiquity to the present through more than 7,000 objects. Two editions take center stage: the 1952 Oslo Winter Games and the 1994 Lillehammer Winter Games. The same ticket includes admission to Maihaugen and the Olympic Museum. Allow 1 hour for it at the end of your visit.

If you enjoy novels, visit Bjerkebæk, Sigrid Undset’s wooden home in Lillehammer. This Norwegian novelist received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1928. Her best-known work, Kristin Lavransdatter, is set in medieval Norway. She lived here from 1919. An opponent of the Nazis, she fled Norway during the German invasion in 1940 and returned in 1945. The house can only be visited on a guided tour, offered several times a day in summer: check the schedule before you go.

Wooden facades, bay windows, and gabled roofs: Storgata, Lillehammer’s main street, is lined with two-story wooden houses from the late 19th century. In 1827, the town was granted market town status, giving it the right to trade. Save this walk for the end of the day. Then head down toward Lake Mjøsa, Norway’s largest lake, with the town at its northern end.

activities.text: You can climb the 936 steps at the Lysgårdsbakken Olympic ski jumps or ride up on the chairlift. The opening and closing ceremonies of the 1994 Winter Games took place at the foot of these ski jumps. The large hill allows jumps of around 140 m. From the top, the views stretch across Lillehammer and Lake Mjøsa. The chairlift generally operates from May through September, and an adult ticket costs 80 NOK.

practical_info.tip: Take the chairlift up and walk back down the stairs alongside the ski jump.

to_next_leg.road_type: E6 through the Gudbrandsdal Valley

visits.text: A medieval timber frame and a 17th-century bell tower: Ringebu Stave Church brings together two eras. It dates from around 1220. Around 1630, carpenter Werner Olsen enlarged it into a cross-shaped church, then added the red bell tower in 1631. Inside, a statue of Saint Lawrence dates from the 13th century. The church is open to visitors from June through August for a small admission fee, and its grounds remain freely accessible year-round.

to_next_leg.road_type: E6 to Otta, then Rv15 toward Lom

visits.text: Lom Stave Church has stood in the center of the village since the 12th century: the timber used for its frame was felled during the winter of 1157–1158. It was enlarged in 1634 and again in the 1660s, giving it its cross-shaped layout. The dragon heads on the roof are copies, and the originals are displayed near the parking lot. Excavations here in 1973 uncovered 2,245 coins, a record for a Norwegian church. Admission costs around 90 NOK, from June through September.

More than half of the archaeological objects found in ice worldwide come from the mountains around Lom. Norsk Fjellsenter, the Norwegian Mountain Center, displays around a hundred of them in its Frozen in Time exhibition. The cold preserved these objects for millennia, and melting ice is revealing them again. You will see a 6,000-year-old arrow and a Viking Age mitten. The center also welcomes visitors to Jotunheimen National Park: pick up maps and advice for Besseggen here.

Crystals, polished stones, and fossils fill the display cases at Fossheim Steinsenter, Lom’s stone center. Its collections bring together minerals from more than 700 Norwegian deposits. The center also displays a meteorite around 4.6 billion years old, which it presents as the oldest stone in the world. Outside the door, a pile of stones replenished daily awaits children, who can take some. Half an hour is enough.

For a break in Lom, nothing beats the banks of the Bøvra. In the village center, this river forms Prestfossen waterfall before joining the Otta River. On the banks of the same river, Bakeriet i Lom bakes its bread in two large wood-fired ovens. This bakery was founded by Morten Schakenda, a former fine-dining chef. Pick up a sandwich and settle in facing the water.

activities.text: Follow Bordvassvegen, an easy trail along an old irrigation canal above Lom. There is very little rain here: many parts of Lom and the neighboring municipality of Skjåk receive less than 300 mm a year. To grow crops, farmers dug canals to bring glacial meltwater to their fields. Lom has 68 canals and small dams, with canals totaling about 230 km in length. The trailhead sign is behind Norsk Fjellsenter, and the trail markings are red.

practical_info.tip: The full route takes 1 to 4 hours: 1 hour is enough to explore the first section and return.

to_next_leg.road_type: Fv55, Sognefjellet scenic route

visits.text: At 1,434 m, Fantesteinen marks the highest point on the Sognefjellet road. The official Norwegian Scenic Routes website describes it as the highest road pass in Northern Europe. The modern road opened in 1938. In the mid-1930s, young unemployed workers had dug part of it using shovels, pickaxes, and wheelbarrows. In spring, walls of snow nearly 10 m high still line the road. In July, afternoon temperatures average barely 11 °C: bring a jacket.

A sculpted block of stone stands out against the bare plateau: it is a work by artist Knut Wold at the Mefjellet rest area. This stop on the Sognefjellet road lies in the middle of the plateau. On a clear day, you can see the Fannaråken glacier and nearby peaks. Stop for 15 minutes: the rest area is wheelchair accessible.

In our opinion, Oscarshaug offers the finest view along the Sognefjellet road. The site is named after King Oscar II, who crossed the mountain in 1860. A cairn, a pile of stones used as a landmark, was erected to commemorate his passage. A path with a steel handrail leads there from the parking lot. Across from you, you will see the Hurrungane massif and the peak of Store Skagastølstind. Turn around here or at Turtagrø, 66 km from Lom, for the return trip.

activities.text: If the sky is clear, start with Galdhøpiggvegen, the toll road that climbs from Galdesand, at 550 m, to Juvasshytta, at the end of the road at 1,841 m. It gains about 1,300 m over 15 km. It is the highest paved road in Northern Europe: it climbs higher than Sognefjellet, but ends in a dead end without crossing a pass. Juvasshytta is a starting point for Galdhøpiggen, Northern Europe’s highest peak at 2,469 m.

practical_info.tip: The toll is 100 NOK per car, payable by card. The road is open from mid-May to late October, depending on the weather. The Sognefjellet road is closed in winter between Bøverdalen and Turtagrø: it reopened on April 2 in 2026, and may still close at night or in bad weather.

to_next_leg.road_type: Return to Lom via Fv55, then Rv15 and Fv51

activities.text: The water of Lake Gjende is a milky green. This color comes from rock flour: a very fine powder ground by glaciers and carried into the lake by the Muru River. From Gjendesheim, at the eastern end of the lake, the boat takes you to Memurubu, the starting point for Besseggen. A one-way ticket costs 260 NOK per adult. Buy your ticket online and take a screenshot, as cell phone reception is poor in places.

practical_info.tip: The boat runs from early June through September (June 6 to September 13 in 2026), with up to seven departures a day to Memurubu. A shuttle connects the long-term parking lot at Reinsvangen, 1.7 km from the dock, with the boat.

activities.text: You will hike back from Memurubu to Gjendesheim along the Besseggen ridge: about 14 km, nearly 1,000 m of ascent, and 6 to 8 hours including breaks. On the ridge, you walk between two lakes: green Gjende and blue Bessvatnet, perched nearly 400 m higher. The highest point, Veslfjellet, reaches 1,743 m. In Henrik Ibsen’s play Peer Gynt, the hero tells of crossing this ridge on the back of a reindeer. Bring at least one liter of water, a windbreaker, and a map.

practical_info.tip: The ridge is steep and narrow. If you feel dizzy at heights, return to Memurubu: the last boat to Gjendesheim leaves at 4:50 p.m., or 5:55 p.m. in peak season.

to_next_leg.road_type: Fv51, Valdresflye scenic route

visits.text: A work of art or a whim of nature? At Steinplassen, on the Valdresflye road, two boulders stacked one on top of the other form the installation Rock on Top of Another Rock (a rock on top of another rock). It is the work of artists Peter Fischli and David Weiss. The piece recalls cairns, the piles of stones hikers stack to mark a trail or a summit. Stop for ten minutes.

Flye 1389, a rest area with a café, takes its name from the elevation of the highest point on Valdresflye, the scenic route crossing this high plateau. In Norwegian, the word “flye” means a flat mountain plateau. The café, which opened in 2020, serves products from Valdres and Gudbrandsdal, such as waffles, cheese, and dried meat. In clear weather, the view stretches across the peaks of Jotunheimen, including Besshøe and Tjønnholstinden. Take your lunch break here.

to_next_leg.road_type: Fv51 via Beitostølen

visits.text: Norwegians call their traditional festive costume a “bunad.” The national institute devoted to these costumes is housed at Valdres Folkemuseum, the open-air museum in Fagernes. Founded in 1901, the museum brings together more than 100 historic buildings and structures on a peninsula in Lake Strondafjorden, 800 m from the center. Pigs, chickens, and sheep roam between the farms. Allow 2 hours. In midsummer, the museum is open daily from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., and an adult ticket costs 140 NOK.

activities.text: You will end the day on Vesleøya, an uninhabited islet connected to the shore in Fagernes by a small white wooden footbridge. It lies about 50 m from the shore of Lake Strondafjorden. It makes for a short, peaceful evening walk, just a few minutes on foot from the center.

practical_info.tip: Allow 15 minutes round-trip.

activities.text: Long before airplanes, Gardermoen was a Norwegian army camp, dating back to 1740. The first flight took place here in 1912. The site became Oslo’s main airport on October 8, 1998, when the old Fornebu Airport closed. From Fagernes, allow for about 165 km and a little over two hours of driving. Leave extra time to refuel and return your rental car.

practical_info.tip: Check the return time listed in your rental agreement.

seo.h1_title: Norway’s Mountains in 5 Days: Lillehammer and Jotunheimen
seo.intro_paragraph: This 5-day loop starts and ends at Oslo Gardermoen Airport, taking you through Lillehammer, Gudbrandsdal Valley, and Lom. You cross Sognefjellet Pass, hike along Besseggen ridge above Lake Gjende, then descend via the Valdresflye plateau to Fagernes.

itineraries.title: Helgeland Coast in 5 Days: Torghatten, Vega, and Svartisen
itineraries.subtitle: Over 5 days, follow the Fv17 coastal road from Brønnøysund to Bodø, with ferries, the Vega islands, and the Svartisen glacier along the way.
itineraries.notes: The shuttle boat to Engabreen glacier runs from May 29 to September 27, 2026, with weekend service only in September, and several museums open only between mid-June and mid-August. Ferries cannot be reserved: in summer, arrive at least 30 minutes before departure.
itineraries.climate: Visit from mid-June to mid-August: in Brønnøysund, July temperatures range from about 10 to 16 °C, with up to 23 hours of daylight. Bring a windbreaker and rain gear, even in midsummer. Avoid November through March: walking through the hole in Torghatten is discouraged then, the Vega stairs become slippery, and daylight lasts only a few hours.

activities.text: Few mountains can be walked through: Torghatten is one of them. This 258 m peak is pierced by a natural tunnel 160 m long and 35 m high. During the ice ages, ice and water wore away the soft rock in the middle. The harder rock at the top held firm. From the parking lot above the campground, allow 15 to 30 minutes for the somewhat steep climb to the hole, and 1 hour to 1 hour 30 minutes for the full round trip.

practical_info.tip: Brønnøysund Airport is 2 km from the town center, and Torghatten is 12 km away. Walking through the hole is discouraged from November through March. A steep, exposed trail leads to the summit: wear sturdy hiking shoes.

activities.text: See farmed salmon up close at Norsk Havbrukssenter, a center devoted to fish farming in Toft. Like Torghatten, it is on the other side of the Brønnøysund bridge. A walkway connects the shore to the fish farm. Using underwater cameras, the guide shows how salmon grow from eggs to adults. You then watch the fish being fed.

practical_info.tip: Visits are guided: check tour times before you come. An on-site restaurant serves local products.

visits.text: As early as around 1200, a church stood on the site of Brønnøy kirke in central Brønnøysund. The current cross-shaped building, made of brown stone, dates from 1870. It replaced the old church, which was damaged by fires in 1772 and 1866. Its oldest object is a wooden crucifix dating from before the Protestant Reformation. Allow 30 minutes: the church is a few minutes’ walk from the harbor.

Havnegata, Brønnøysund’s harbor street, is the best place to watch daily life in this town of about 5,000 residents. Small boats come and go between the islands. Every day, the Hurtigruten, the coastal express that travels along Norway’s coast, calls at the dock. Throughout the country, the town is best known for Brønnøysundregistrene, the agency that maintains Norway’s business register. Come in the afternoon, when the southbound Hurtigruten calls.

activities.text: The scent of herbs greets you at the entrance to Hildurs Urterarium, an herb garden in Tilrem, about 7 km from Brønnøysund. Hildur and her husband handed their farm over to the next generation in 1988. She then created this garden and its restaurant. The plants are grouped by theme: culinary herbs, medicinal plants, and heirloom varieties. The roughly 250-year-old farmhouse stands in the shade of a 150-year-old elm.

practical_info.tip: The garden is open from May 15 to September 30. It is on the road to the Vega ferry: stop here before boarding at Horn.

to_next_leg.road_type: Drive to the Horn ferry dock, take the Horn–Igerøy ferry (50 minutes), then drive to Gladstad
to_next_leg.justification: Segment 1: drive from Brønnøysund to the Horn ferry dock; segment 2: Horn–Igerøy ferry, 50 minutes (fergeruter.info); segment 3: drive from Igerøy to Gladstad on Vega; about 38 km total (bikemap) and an estimated 30 minutes of driving, excluding waiting time.

visits.text: If you visit just one place on Vega, choose Vega verdensarvsenter, the World Heritage Center in Gardsøy. The archipelago has been UNESCO-listed since 2004 for a 1,500-year-old tradition. Residents build small shelters where eiders, wild sea ducks, nest each spring. Once the young have left, the down remaining in the nests is collected. Opened in 2019, the center takes 45 minutes to 2 hours to visit and offers free parking.

Small but packed with details, E-huset in Nes is a museum devoted to the eider, housed in a former store in this fishing hamlet. The original counter is still there, along with shelves filled with goods from days gone by. The museum tells the story of Vega’s residents as guardians of the migratory birds that nest on the island. Nes is about 16 km from the Igerøy dock. Call before you come: hours vary by season.

activities.text: Climb Vegatrappa, a stone staircase with more than a thousand steps, to the summit of Ravnfloget on Vega’s west coast. The walk covers 950 m with about 310 m of elevation gain and takes 30 to 60 minutes each way. At the top, views stretch across the archipelago and the island of Søla. Vega lies south of the Arctic Circle. Yet the atmosphere bends the sun’s rays, making it appear slightly higher than it actually is: this is refraction. Thanks to this effect, you can see the midnight sun in midsummer.

practical_info.tip: Save some energy for the descent. The staircase is closed in winter because the steps become very slippery.

activities.text: Sand beneath your feet at 65 degrees north latitude: Kjulstranda, on Vega’s southeast coast, is a sandy beach well suited to swimming. The shallow water is also good for playing and snorkeling. An open wooden shelter with a fire pit provides a place to picnic. The parking lot is small, so arrive early on days with good weather.

practical_info.tip: On busy days, bike from the Rørøy express boat dock: allow about 30 minutes at a leisurely pace.

to_next_leg.road_type: Drive to the Igerøy ferry dock, take the Igerøy–Tjøtta ferry (about 1 hour), then drive to Alstahaug
to_next_leg.justification: Segment 1: drive from Gladstad to the Igerøy dock, about 15 minutes; segment 2: direct Igerøy–Tjøtta ferry, about 1 hour (fergeruter.info), with few departures; segment 3: drive from Tjøtta to Alstahaug, about 10 minutes; if no direct departure works, return via Horn.

visits.text: All graves are anonymous at Tjøtta internasjonale krigskirkegård, the Tjøtta International War Cemetery, established in 1970. Those buried here include victims of the Rigel, a cargo ship requisitioned by the German army. On November 27, 1944, British aircraft bombed it, believing they were targeting German soldiers. Most of those aboard were Russian, Serbian, and Polish prisoners of war. More than 2,500 people died. The cemetery, between Tjøtta and Sandnessjøen, has a rest area with parking.

Although designed primarily for Norwegian visitors, the Petter Dass-museet is worth a stop, at least for its building, designed by the architecture firm Snøhetta and opened in 2007. Petter Dass was the pastor of Alstahaug from 1689 until his death in 1707. The poet described northern Norway in verse in The Trumpet of Nordland. For a hundred years after his death, many fishing boats in the north carried a black cloth in their sails as a sign of mourning. The museum is closed on Mondays.

Alstahaug kirke, next to the museum, is one of seven medieval churches still standing in northern Norway. It was completed around 1150, partly using locally sourced soapstone, a soft rock that is easy to carve. The small onion dome above the roof dates from a later restoration. The site's historic buildings, including the parsonage from the mid-18th century, are open from June through August, or by appointment.

activities.text: According to legend, De syv søstre, the Seven Sisters, are troll sisters chased along the coast by another troll, the Horseman. The first rays of sunlight turned them to stone. The mountain range rises to 1,072 m east of Sandnessjøen. From the Markvoll parking lot, 4.7 km from Søvik, a marked 1.5 km trail climbs 250 m to Markvollkulpen, a series of natural pools and a small waterfall at the foot of Skjæringen and Tvillingan.

practical_info.tip: Allow 30 to 60 minutes one way, with sections that are steep and slippery in wet weather. To reach a summit, Skjæringen (1,037 m), the easiest, takes 4 to 5 hours round-trip from Markvoll.

visits.text: Step through the doorway of a 65 m longhouse at Høvdingsetet på Sandnes, a reconstructed Viking chieftain's estate less than a kilometer from downtown Sandnessjøen. A longhouse is the large wooden house typical of the Viking Age. This one was rebuilt on the site of the Viking Age building. The Sandnes estate appears in Egil's Saga, an Icelandic narrative. The site opens at set times in summer and by appointment for groups during the rest of the year.

Large murals decorate downtown Sandnessjøen, including Future Eyes, created in 2016 by Jort Agoch and Leticia Cascone Ruiz. Along the way, you will pass statues of Petter Dass and the Seven Sisters. Kulturbadet, which opened that same year, houses a swimming pool, movie theater, and library. One street is named after Torolv Kveldulvsson, a Viking chieftain who exported stockfish, or air-dried fish. Park near the harbor and explore downtown on foot.

At 1,065 m long, Helgelandsbrua, the Helgeland Bridge, has connected the island of Alsta, where Sandnessjøen is located, to the mainland since July 1991. It is a cable-stayed bridge: cables stretched from tall pylons support the roadway. Its longest span measures 425 m. Boats have up to 45 m of clearance beneath the roadway. You will cross it as you leave Sandnessjøen for the Levang ferry, and the crossing has been toll-free since 2005.

to_next_leg.road_type: Helgeland Bridge to Levang, Levang–Nesna ferry (30 minutes), then Fv17 north
to_next_leg.justification: Segment 1: drive from Sandnessjøen to Levang via the Helgeland Bridge, about 20 km in 20 minutes; segment 2: Levang–Nesna ferry, about 30 minutes; segment 3: Fv17 from Nesna to Grønsvik, about 68 km in 70 minutes; driving is the main mode by duration, and the previous value combined travel and waiting time.

visits.text: Grønsvik kystfort, a coastal fort beside Fv17, was part of the Atlantic Wall. This chain of German fortifications stretched from the French-Spanish border to northern Norway. The occupying forces made 77 Soviet prisoners and 65 Polish prisoners build it. They excavated rooms and tunnels in the rock. Seven Soviet prisoners died during construction; their remains are buried in Tjøtta Cemetery. The fort is 2 km north of the Stokkvågen junction.

activities.text: If you stay on the ferry's deck between Kilboghamn and Jektvik, you will cross the Arctic Circle. A globe on the small islet of Vikingen marks this line. It is illuminated at night and serves as a landmark for sailors. The Arctic Circle is the theoretical boundary beyond which the midnight sun can be seen. The crew generally announces the crossing during the trip, which takes a little over an hour.

practical_info.tip: Departures on this route are limited: check the schedule before leaving Grønsvik, about a 45-minute drive from the Kilboghamn dock.

to_next_leg.road_type: Fv17 to Kilboghamn, Kilboghamn–Jektvik ferry across the Arctic Circle, drive to Ågskardet, then Ågskardet–Forøy ferry
to_next_leg.justification: Segment 1: Fv17 from Grønsvik to Kilboghamn, about 45 minutes; segment 2: Kilboghamn–Jektvik ferry, about 1 hour 5 minutes; segment 3: drive from Jektvik to Ågskardet, 27.5 km in 24 minutes; segment 4: Ågskardet–Forøy ferry, about 10 minutes, then a few minutes to Halsa; the ferries account for as much travel time as driving and determine the schedule, hence the ferry mode.

visits.text: One of the best roadside views of Svartisen is from the Braset picnic area, just south of Holandsvika. Svartisen is Norway's second-largest glacier. Its name comes from svart, “black,” and is, “ice”: the old ice here looks darker than fresh snow. Stop on your way to catch the boat from Holandsvika, camera in hand.

activities.text: You will stay overnight in Halsa, a village in Meløy along Fv17, just after the ten-minute ferry crossing of the fjord from Ågskardet. Halsa is the most convenient base for Engabreen. Boats to the glacier leave from Holandsvika, about ten kilometers away. In summer, the first boat leaves at 10 a.m.

practical_info.tip: Before June 19 and after August 16, 2026, the 10 a.m. boat must be booked online the day before, before 8 p.m.

to_next_leg.road_type: Fv17 to Holandsvika, then the Isprins boat across Holandsfjord
to_next_leg.justification: Segment 1: Fv17 from Halsa to Holandsvika, approximately 12 km in 12 minutes; segment 2: Isprins shuttle across Holandsfjord, approximately 15 minutes (tilsvartisen.no); the walk to the glacier is included in the stop, not in the travel time.

visits.text: Between 1999 and 2022, the Engabreen glacier front retreated approximately 700 m, according to the Norwegian Water Resources and Energy Directorate (NVE). Engabreen is a tongue of the Svartisen glacier—an arm of ice descending from the plateau. It once reached almost all the way to the fjord. Today, it ends at an elevation of around 110 m, above Lake Engabrevatnet. Beneath the ice, a laboratory allows researchers to observe the glacier bed under nearly 200 m of ice. Stay at the cairn, the pile of stones marking the end of the trail: blocks of ice can fall without warning.

activities.text: You will cross Holandsfjorden in 15 minutes aboard Isprins, the shuttle departing from Holandsvika. From the dock at Engen, a gravel track follows Lake Engabrevatnet for 3 km. A rocky trail then leads to the cairn, 4.3 km from the dock. Allow 1 hour 30 minutes to 2 hours each way, with approximately 190 m of elevation gain. The last 500 meters are the steepest.

practical_info.tip: In 2026, the shuttle runs from May 29 to September 27, with weekend service only in September, at a round-trip fare of 275 kroner per adult. Bikes can be rented at the dockside kiosk for the gravel track section. Keep at least 100 m between you and the glacier front.

activities.text: Svartisgryta, approximately 600 m beyond the cairn, is a glacial pothole: a large, round hollow carved into the rock by ice and water. In warm weather, some hikers swim in it. The detour follows a marked trail and adds 30 minutes to the walk to Engabreen.

practical_info.tip: Before continuing, check the departure time of the last boat from Engen.

activities.text: If the wind picks up, Brestua, the summer café on the shore of Lake Engabrevatnet, offers a break with views of Engabreen. It is a 15- or 20-minute walk from the dock at Engen, near the start of the hike. It is a good place to warm up on your return from the glacier. This café is open only in summer.

practical_info.tip: Keep an eye on the time: during the 2026 peak season, the last boat leaves Engen at 7:45 p.m.

to_next_leg.road_type: Isprins boat to Holandsvika, then Fv17 through the Svartisen Tunnel to Ørnes
to_next_leg.justification: Segment 1: Isprins shuttle from Engen to Holandsvika, approximately 15 minutes; segment 2: Fv17 from Holandsvika to Ørnes through the Svartisen Tunnel, approximately 45 km in 45 minutes; driving is the main mode of transportation, as the shuttle ride takes only 15 minutes.

visits.text: In 1794, boat skipper Elling Pedersen obtained permission to open a shop and an inn in Ørnes. Three buildings remain from this former trading post, Ørnes handelssted: the main house, the old bakery, and the forge. They have been protected since 1942. The site served as the village’s gathering place for many years. In 2026, it is open Monday through Saturday, from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m., from June 20 to August 8.

The most enjoyable way to spend time in Ørnes, the administrative center of Meløy municipality, is to stroll among the old harbor buildings. Several date from around 1800: houses, fishermen’s cabins, boathouses, barns, and a forge, some of which are protected. The island of Mesøya lies just west of the village. Hurtigruten calls here daily. Park near the dock and explore on foot in 30 minutes.

to_next_leg.road_type: Fv17 along the coast to Bodø

activities.text: You will reach Bodø via Fv17, approximately 116 km from Ørnes, a drive of just under 2 hours. Bodø Airport is just south of downtown. Return your rental car there before your flight. Leave early if your flight departs around midday, as photo stops along the coast take time.

practical_info.tip: This itinerary ends at the airport: allow extra time to return the car.

itineraries.title: Vesterålen in 4 Days: Andenes Whales, Bleik, and Nyksund
itineraries.subtitle: In 4 days, travel from Sortland to the villages of Stø and Nyksund, then follow the coast of Andøya to the whales of Andenes.
itineraries.notes: This itinerary is designed for June through August, the season for the Queen’s Route, the puffins of Bleiksøya, and the Andøya Space center. It ends in Andenes, whose airport has connections to Evenes, Bodø, and Tromsø. From mid-May through late September, its port also has a summer ferry to Gryllefjord, on the island of Senja, with no reservations (a crossing of 1 hour 40 minutes).
itineraries.climate: Visit from June through August: in Andenes, average highs range from 11 °C in June to 14 °C in July and August, with nighttime temperatures around 7 to 9 °C. Avoid September for hiking: it is significantly rainier than the summer months. Pack a windbreaker, a fleece, and rain gear, even in July; in winter, the sun does not rise from early December to early January.

activities.text: Pick up your rental car at Harstad/Narvik Airport, Evenes, the starting point for this itinerary through Vesterålen. Allow about 1 hour 40 minutes for the 121 km drive to Sortland. The E10 first crosses the Tjeldsund Bridge, then you head toward Gullesfjord. The Rv85 then takes you north to the blue town. In summer, the sun barely sets at these latitudes: even an evening arrival leaves enough daylight to enjoy the drive.

practical_info.tip: If you are departing from Andenes, book a “one-way” rental: fees generally apply when you return the car to a different location.

to_next_leg.road_type: E10 via the Tjeldsund Bridge, then Rv85

visits.text: From pale blue to deep blue, Sortland’s facades display every shade of a single color. This art project is called Blåbyen, “the blue town.” The idea came from a local artist, Bjørn Elvenes. The mayor presented it in 1998, and the municipality then adopted it as its project for the year 2000, despite residents’ initially mixed reactions. On some walls, look for short poems written by children and Lars Saabye Christensen, one of Norway’s best-known writers. An hour on foot is enough to explore the town center.

Look for the white bell tower rising south of the quay: it belongs to Sortland Church (Sortland kirke). A succession of places of worship has stood on this site since the 14th century. The current building dates from 1901. Its white exterior contrasts with the blue facades of the town center, making it a useful landmark for finding your way around. Allow about twenty minutes, before or after the walk toward the bridge.

activities.text: The opening of the Sortland Bridge (Sortlandsbrua) in 1975 greatly improved access to the entire region. It connects Langøya, the island where the town stands, to Hinnøya, the largest island in the archipelago. Walk along the waterfront to see both the bridge and the blue facades, which are visible from far out in the strait. Every day, the Hurtigruten coastal ship, which serves ports along the Norwegian coast, calls at Sortland: 15 minutes northbound and 30 minutes southbound.

practical_info.tip: Check the Hurtigruten schedule if you want to watch the ship dock.

visits.text: Stø is a fishing village at the northernmost tip of Langøya, where the road ends facing the open sea. A radar station is visible on the nearby mountain. Offshore lies the Stø and Nyksund Nature Reserve, an important nesting site for seabirds. Walk around the harbor before setting off on your hike. If you prefer the sea to hiking, Arctic Whale Tours offers a 6 to 8 hour whale-watching day trip from June through August, departing at 10 a.m.

activities.text: Norwegians call it Dronningruta, “the Queen’s Route,” because Queen Sonja first hiked it in 1994. From Stø, this 12.3 km loop initially follows the coast, passing white-sand beaches and Skipssanden Beach. It then climbs onto a ridge to Finngamheia, its highest point, before descending back to the village. Allow about 5 hours of hiking, with 665 m of elevation gain. There are no springs along the route: bring enough water.

practical_info.tip: The trail is marked with red T’s and recommended from June through September; bring a windbreaker and sturdy footwear, as the terrain is exposed.

to_next_leg.road_type: Narrow single-lane road for the last 10 km
to_next_leg.justification: Nyksund is on a peninsula with no direct road from Stø: you need to head back south toward Myre, then take the small road to Nyksund, so the stated detour of 25 km in 35 minutes is accurate.

visits.text: Once a ghost village, now an artists’ haven: Nyksund has had two lives. Around 1900, it was Vesterålen’s second-largest fishing port, bustling with nearly 1,000 people during the fishing season. As boats grew larger, its narrow harbor could no longer accommodate them, and residents moved away. The last resident left the village in 1975. Nyksund occupies two islets, Ungsmaløy and Nyksundøy, connected by a causeway. Park in the parking lot at the entrance: the narrow, steep lanes are explored on foot.

activities.text: In 1985, young people from Berlin began bringing Nyksund back to life. Launched by German educator Karl Heinz Nickel, the project gave disadvantaged young people practical work: repainting, clearing debris, and repairing houses. For about ten years, hundreds of young Europeans took turns working here in summer. Today, artists and musicians live here. Stroll between the two art galleries and Delpen, a bookstore and café selling books from northern Norway and antiques.

practical_info.tip: Concerts and exhibitions are held here regularly in summer; some venues open only seasonally or on request.

to_next_leg.road_type: Via Sortland, then Fv82 toward Andøya
to_next_leg.justification: There is no bridge or ferry across the stretch of sea between Nyksund and Risøyhamn: the road goes around via Myre and Sortland, then follows Fv82, making it about 100 km for a straight-line distance of 25 km. The current figure is correct.

visits.text: If you arrive via Andøybrua, the 750 m bridge leading to the village of Risøyhamn, look down at the strait below. According to local tradition, it was once so shallow that people crossed it on horseback at low tide. To let ships through, a channel nearly 5 km long, the Risøyrenna, was dredged and opened in 1922. Richard With, founder of Hurtigruten, the Norwegian coastal shipping line, had long called for this channel. A 15-minute stop in the village is enough.

activities.text: Take your time driving the Andøya National Scenic Route (Nasjonal turistveg Andøya), which begins in Bjørnskinn, very close to the bridge. For 58 km to Andenes, it follows the west coast between the mountains and the ocean. Seals, whales, and white-tailed eagles, large sea eagles, can sometimes be seen from the car. Stop at designated rest areas such as Kleivodden, from which you can see Bleik and the island of Bleiksøya. Near Børvågen, operations at the Andøya Spaceport satellite launch facility can close the road for up to 8 hours.

practical_info.tip: The road information service (+47 815 48 991) reports road closures related to launches.

to_next_leg.road_type: Andøya National Scenic Route

activities.text: Måtinden rises to just 408 m, but its summit drops sheer into the ocean. It is Andøya’s most visited mountain. The trail starts at a parking lot on the road between Stave and Bleik. It first crosses a peat bog, an area of spongy, waterlogged ground, before tackling its steepest, rockiest section. From the summit, the view takes in white beaches, the open sea, and Bleiksøya, the bird island. Allow 3 to 4 hours for the roughly 8 km round trip. At the top, stay well back from the cliff edge. Hike up in the evening to enjoy the midnight sun.

practical_info.tip: Free roadside parking about 5 km south of Bleik; bring waterproof hiking boots, from mid-May to mid-October.

visits.text: In Norwegian, “bleik” means pale: the white sand of Bleikstranda gave the village its name. This beach, just north of the houses, is among Norway’s longest. Walk along it in the evening, when the midnight sun lights up the sand and the silhouette of Bleiksøya island. The water stays very cold, even in midsummer: swimming is for the brave.

Bleik’s biggest surprise lies beneath your feet. The northern part of the village is built on a gårdshaug, a mound formed by the remains of farms and waste accumulated in the same place over centuries. Here, these layers reach a thickness of 6 m, the greatest depth measured in Norway for this type of mound. The village had to rebuild after a violent storm destroyed much of it in 1925. A 30-minute walk to the harbor and its breakwater is enough to look around.

activities.text: Seen from the beach, Bleiksøya island looks like a cone sitting on the sea, about 160 m high. Its cliffs host around 80,000 pairs of Atlantic puffins, small seabirds with colorful bills, from mid-April to early August. The island is a nature reserve where landing is prohibited. The boat operated by Puffin Safari, based in Bleik, reaches the colony in ten minutes. A white-tailed eagle, a large sea eagle, can eat about two puffins a day here in summer. Prices start at 800 Norwegian kroner.

practical_info.tip: Trips run from mid-April to early August; book online and leave some flexibility in your schedule, as wind can cause cancellations.

visits.text: Stop by the Whale Center, the safari visitor center at Andenes harbor, before boarding. Its whale exhibition is included with every Whalesafari Andenes ticket. It introduces the species living offshore and the ocean conditions around the island. A one-hour guided tour is available for an additional 150 Norwegian kroner. A large center devoted to whales, The Whale, will also open in Andenes starting June 4, 2027. Arrive early: safari check-in takes place at the Whale Center.

Bright red against the pale sky, Andenes Lighthouse (Andenes fyr) rises 40 m above the northern tip of Andøya. Its cast-iron tower was assembled on-site from plates in the mid-19th century. Right next door, Andøymuseet tells the story of Hilmar Nøis, a trapper, or fur hunter. He spent 38 winters on Spitsbergen, the main island of the Svalbard archipelago. In summer, the museum offers guided climbs to the top of the lighthouse: 148 steps. Ask at the front desk for times.

Andenes’s most unexpected detour leads toward space. Andøya Space is Norway’s only active space center: research rockets have launched here since 1962. Its visitor center, Spaceship Aurora, explains the northern lights through an exhibition and a film. The virtual role-playing game Journey to Mars lets you spend 70 minutes in teams of six playing researchers sent to find out whether life exists on Mars. It is recommended for ages 10 and up. The center is open from May through late September: book online in summer.

activities.text: If you take just one boat trip, make it a whale-watching safari from Andenes. Very close to shore, the seabed plunges abruptly into an underwater canyon, Bleiksdjupet. The cold water rising from this canyon is rich in food. Male sperm whales live here year-round, diving very deep to hunt squid. Females stay in warmer waters, such as those around the Azores. From May to September, Whalesafari Andenes runs trips lasting 3 to 4 hours aboard a traditional boat. If you see neither a whale nor a dolphin, you are offered another trip free of charge.

practical_info.tip: From October to April, trips use fast inflatable boats and are less frequent and shorter, with limited daylight. Orcas and humpback whales are occasional visitors to Andenes: in winter, they mainly frequent the coast farther north, around Skjervøy. From May to September, Arctic Whale Tours also offers trips lasting 3 to 5 hours aboard the catamaran MS Alba.

seo.h1_title: Vesterålen in 4 Days: Andenes Whales, Bleik, and Nyksund
seo.intro_paragraph: This 4-day road trip starts at Evenes Airport and crosses Vesterålen, an archipelago in northern Norway. You hike the Queen’s Route between Stø and Nyksund, then follow the Andøya National Scenic Route to Bleik and its puffins. The trip ends in Andenes, the departure point for whale-watching safaris.

itineraries.title: Oslo in 2 Days: MUNCH, Vigeland, the Opera House, and Bygdøy
itineraries.subtitle: Explore the Opera House, MUNCH, Vigeland Park, and the museums of Bygdøy in 2 days on foot, by metro, and by ferry.
itineraries.notes: The Viking Ship Museum on Bygdøy is being rebuilt and is scheduled to reopen in 2027 as the Museum of the Viking Age. The museum ferry runs from mid-March to early October; during the rest of the year, bus 30 connects the city center with the museums of Bygdøy.
itineraries.climate: Best time to visit: May to September, with highs of 16 to 23 °C and more than 18 hours of daylight around Midsummer. In winter, daylight lasts only about 6 hours, and January highs hover around 0 °C: bundle up for walks between stops. July, August, and October are the rainiest months, so keep a raincoat in your bag.

visits.text: The best starting point for a weekend in Oslo is the Nasjonalmuseet, the National Museum of Art, Architecture and Design. It opened in June 2022 behind the former West Station. Its Munch room brings together 18 major works by painter Edvard Munch, including the 1893 version of The Scream. On the top floor, the Lyshallen (“Light Hall”) has glass walls enclosing a thin layer of marble. In the evening, it glows like a lamp above the city. Closed on Mondays, the museum stays open until 8 p.m. on Tuesdays and Wednesdays.

to_next_leg.justification: A walk between two nearby stops in the city center; the routing engine calculated a driving route (due to one-way streets, a detour, or a zero distance), but the stated walk of 0.3 km in 5 minutes is correct.

activities.text: Ships were built at Aker Brygge until 1982, when the shipyard closed. The first buildings in the new neighborhood, with restaurants, stores, and homes, were completed in 1986. Follow the waterfront to Tjuvholmen, “Thieves’ Islet”: thieves were executed here in the 18th century. At its tip, a sculpture park designed by architect Renzo Piano sits beside a small swimming area. In summer, tuck a swimsuit into your bag.

practical_info.tip: Ferries from the Aker Brygge terminal go to Nesodden: these are not the museum ferries. The Bygdøy ferry leaves from the nearby pier in front of City Hall (Rådhusbrygge 3).

to_next_leg.road_type: Walk along the harbor
to_next_leg.justification: A walk between two nearby stops in the city center; the routing engine calculated a driving route (due to one-way streets, a detour, or a zero distance), but the stated walk of 0.9 km in 12 minutes is correct.

visits.text: Every hour from 7 a.m. to midnight, the 49 bells of Oslo City Hall (Oslo rådhus) play a tune above the harbor. The building was inaugurated in 1950 to mark the city’s 900th anniversary. Every December 10, it hosts the Nobel Peace Prize ceremony. In the main hall, murals by Henrik Sørensen and Alf Rolfsen depict the history and working lives of Norwegians. Entry is through a security check, Monday through Saturday from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. City Hall is closed on Sundays, so plan this first day for a Saturday.

to_next_leg.justification: A walk between two nearby stops in the city center; the routing engine calculated a driving route (due to one-way streets, a detour, or a zero distance), but the stated walk of 0.8 km in 12 minutes is correct.

visits.text: No foreign army has ever succeeded in taking Akershus Fortress (Akershus festning) by siege. Yet it surrendered without a fight in 1940: faced with the German invasion, the government had just evacuated the capital. King Haakon V had it built toward the end of the 1290s. After a fire in 1624, King Christian IV transformed it into a Renaissance castle. The fortress grounds along the fjord are free to explore. The castle (100 NOK, including an English audio guide) has opening hours that vary by season: check them before visiting.

to_next_leg.road_type: Harbor promenade along the fjord

activities.text: You can walk on the roof of the Oslo Opera House (Operahuset): it slopes down to the level of the plaza, so you can walk up for views of the fjord. Inaugurated on April 12, 2008, the building was designed by Norwegian architecture firm Snøhetta. Its slopes are clad in white granite and white Italian marble. In the water, a glass and steel sculpture, She Lies, floats and moves with the tide and wind. Wear sneakers, as recommended by the Norwegian tourist board.

practical_info.tip: Guided tours in English on Saturdays and Sundays: about 50 minutes, 180 NOK, with tickets going on sale on Tuesday of the same week. The foyer is open during the day from 11 a.m. (noon on Sundays) to 4 p.m.

to_next_leg.justification: A walk between two nearby stops in the city center; the routing engine calculated a driving route (due to one-way streets, a detour, or a zero distance), but the stated walk of 0.4 km in 5 minutes is correct.

visits.text: If you are keen to see The Scream at MUNCH, the Edvard Munch museum, be aware that the version on display changes throughout the day. The museum owns eight versions: one painting, one drawing, and six lithographs (prints made from a drawing on stone). Light fades the colors and damages the paper, so none can remain on permanent display. They take turns on the 4th floor in the Edvard Munch Infinite exhibition. Then head up to the 13th and top floor for views over the city. Open until 9 p.m. Wednesday through Saturday; admission is 220 NOK.

to_next_leg.road_type: Walk to Jernbanetorget, take the subway to Majorstuen, then walk 10 minutes to the park
to_next_leg.justification: Segment 1: about 10 minutes on foot from MUNCH to Jernbanetorget; segment 2: subway from Jernbanetorget to Majorstuen, about 7 minutes; segment 3: 10 minutes on foot to Vigeland Park; about 6 km in 30 minutes, with the subway being the main mode of transportation by distance.

visits.text: Norwegians call him Sinnataggen, “the little hothead”: this furious toddler is one of the most popular statues in Vigeland Park (Vigelandsparken). Sculptor Gustav Vigeland designed the park’s 212 bronze and granite sculptures from the 1920s until his death in 1943. Monolitten, a stone column, stands over 14 m tall. Its 121 human figures were carved from a single block. The park is free and open day and night: come early in the morning to enjoy it in peace.

to_next_leg.road_type: Tram 12, then a ferry from the City Hall pier

visits.text: Traditional music and warm flatbreads: from late June to mid-August, the Norsk Folkemuseum (Norwegian Museum of Cultural History) offers folk dancing every hour and lefse, a soft flatbread. This open-air museum has reassembled more than 150 buildings brought here from towns and rural areas. At its center stands Gol Stave Church, whose timber frame rests on large posts. Its tree rings, the rings a tree forms each year, date it to between 1157 and 1216. Admission is 200 NOK; from October to April, opening hours are 11 a.m. to 4 p.m.

to_next_leg.road_type: On foot via Museumsveien, Bygdøynesveien
to_next_leg.justification: Trajet urbain fait à pied entre norsk folkemuseum et frammuseet, environ 1400 m de marche réelle comptés 2 km : l'ancienne durée de 4 min venait du calcul voiture, elle est remplacée par 19 min de marche.

visits.text: You can board the Fram, the polar ship on display at the Frammuseet. Its rounded hull was designed so that closing ice would lift the ship instead of crushing it. This allowed explorer Fridtjof Nansen to leave it trapped in the Arctic pack ice for nearly three years. Roald Amundsen later sailed it toward Antarctica for his 1910 to 1912 expedition, the first to reach the South Pole. Walk around the hull before heading up on deck. Open daily from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m.; admission is 180 NOK.

to_next_leg.justification: The Fram Museum and the Kon-Tiki Museum face each other on the Bygdøy peninsula: about 100 meters on foot in 2 minutes, an accurate current value; the driving routing engine returned a distance of zero.

visits.text: In 1947, six men crossed the Pacific on a raft made of balsa, a very lightweight wood. This raft, the Kon-Tiki, is on display at the Kon-Tiki Museum (Kon-Tiki Museet), near the Fram. Their leader, Norwegian Thor Heyerdahl, wanted to prove that peoples from South America could have reached Polynesia before Christopher Columbus arrived in the Americas. Setting off from Peru, they sailed for 101 days before striking a reef in the Tuamotu Islands in Polynesia. The museum also displays the Ra II, a reed boat that crossed the Atlantic in 1970. Allow 1 hour; admission is 180 NOK.

seo.h1_title: Oslo in 2 Days: MUNCH, Vigeland, the Opera House, and Bygdøy
seo.intro_paragraph: This 2-day weekend in Oslo is car-free, with travel on foot, by subway, tram, and ferry. The first day follows the harbor from the Nasjonalmuseet to MUNCH, passing Oslo City Hall, Akershus Fortress, and the roof of the Oslo Opera House. The second connects Vigeland Park with the museums on the Bygdøy peninsula.

itineraries.title: Østfold in 3 Days: Fredrikstad, Halden, and the Hvaler Islands
itineraries.subtitle: In 3 days, travel from Fredrikstad’s fortified old town to the Hvaler Islands, then to Halden’s fortress.
itineraries.notes: From Oslo, allow about 1 hour 10 minutes to drive to Fredrikstad, and just over 1 hour 30 minutes to return from Halden by train. The Fredriksten Museum, the national park visitor center, and Rød Manor have reduced hours outside summer: plan your trip between June and August.
itineraries.climate: Aim for June through August: in Fredrikstad, average highs hover around 20 to 21 °C, and the sea reaches 15 to 18 °C. Avoid November through March, when most rock carvings are covered because of frost and the Fredriksten Museum is closed. Fall is the rainiest season, with rainfall peaking in October.

visits.text: Few fortified towns are as easy to explore as Gamlebyen, Fredrikstad’s old town. King Frederik II founded it in 1567 to replace Sarpsborg, the neighboring town burned down by the Swedish army. His statue stands in Kongens torv, the King’s Square. To the southeast, facing the Glomma River, the Provianthuset, a former army provisions storehouse built in 1674, is the district’s oldest surviving building. Shops and artists’ studios are open year-round, even on Sundays.

Beneath your feet, the grassy ramparts form a star around Gamlebyen. This shape follows the Dutch system of bastions, pointed projections from which defenders could fire along the walls. Willem Coucheron drew up the plans, and construction began in 1663. The moats are more than 40 m wide in places. They are shallow, but a deeper channel runs down the middle to prevent enemies from wading across. You can walk around the ramparts freely, day or night.

Gamlebyen’s largest building was once a military equipment warehouse: the Tøihuset, built in 1775, now houses the Fredrikstad Museum. On the ground floor, “Bar 1567” presents the city’s history interactively, as though a bartender were telling it to customers. Upstairs, a timeline connects the objects on display with the stories of local residents. An exhibition covering more than 500 m² traces the German invasion of Østfold in April 1940 and the local resistance. Admission costs 120 Norwegian kroner (NOK) per adult.

To see Gamlebyen from above, walk to Kongsten Fort, about 500 m east of the old town. It was built around 1680 on Galgeberget, “Gallows Hill.” The fort prevented enemies from occupying this high ground, where their cannons would have commanded the town and had a longer range. Today, the view stretches across Fredrikstad and the surrounding countryside. Head up late in the day, after visiting the museums.

Fredrikstad domkirke, a red-brick cathedral, stands in the modern city center on the west bank of the Glomma River. It was consecrated in 1880 and built in a Gothic Revival style modeled on medieval churches. Its spire rises to 72 m. In the chancel, Emanuel Vigeland’s stained-glass windows date from 1917 and depict angels playing music and the parable of the prodigal son. The church was only named a cathedral in 1969. Stop by just after taking the ferry across from Gamlebyen.

Long before Gamlebyen, there was Isegran, a small green island in the middle of the Glomma River. It is the first place in Fredrikstad mentioned in the archives: in the late 13th century, Count Alv Erlingsson maintained a small fortress here. Until 1680, the island was Norway’s only naval port. Wooden boats are restored here today, and the island is home to the country’s only school of traditional boatbuilding. Reach it on foot via the Kråkerøy Bridge or take the city ferry.

activities.text: The shortest crossing of the trip is also one of the most enjoyable: the Gamlebyfergen connects Cicignon, on the west bank of the Glomma River, to Gamlebyen in about one minute. This city ferry is free, including for bicycles. Fredrikstad municipality introduced its first motorized ferries in the early 1930s. Each boat carries a maximum of 50 passengers. On busy days, a full ferry may therefore pass the dock without stopping.

practical_info.tip: Ferry schedules are published by Fredrikstad municipality under byfergene.

activities.text: You can also spend longer on the water. Another free municipal ferry travels down the Glomma River from Gamlebyen to Ålekilen in about 22 minutes. It stops at Smertu, the city center, Værste, and Gressvik. This lets you watch both banks of Fredrikstad drift by without paying for a ticket. For the return trip, you must get off at the last stop and line up again.

practical_info.tip: In summer and on public holidays, expect a wait at the last stop before you can board again.

to_next_leg.road_type: Route 108, bridges, and the Hvaler Tunnel

map_keywords: Ytre Hvaler National Park Center Skjærhalden

visits.text: The Ytre Hvaler National Park visitor center occupies the Kornmagasinet, the former grain storehouse in Skjærhalden’s harbor. Established in 2009, this was Norway’s first marine national park. Of its 354 km², only 14 are land: all the rest lies beneath the sea. Among its protected features is the 1,200 m-long Tisler coral reef. The center’s exhibition explains this underwater world. From early June to mid-August, the center is open daily from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m.

With its rectangular stone nave and narrow chancel ending in a rounded apse, Hvaler kirke, or Hvaler Church, has the simple appearance of a medieval church. Construction probably began between the years 1000 and 1100. The church gave the island of Kirkøy its name, meaning “Church Island.” Inside, the pulpit dates from the 1600s and the altarpiece from 1759. Save your visit for late in the day, after the coastal trail.

activities.text: Set aside the afternoon for the Kyststien, Kirkøy’s coastal trail: an 11.4 km loop starting at the national park visitor center in Skjærhalden. Blue trail markers lead to Homlungen Lighthouse, a protected monument, then to Storesand Beach and its summer snack bar. The trail then crosses the old pine forest of Prestegårdsskogen, a nature reserve. At Rødshue, a former quarry displays works by five international sculptors. Allow about 3 hours of walking on sand, smooth rocks, and forest paths.

practical_info.tip: The trail can be walked from May through October. If you are traveling by boat, be aware that landing in protected seabird nesting areas is prohibited from April 15 to July 15. Fires are prohibited from April 15 to September 15.

to_next_leg.road_type: Route 110, the Oldtidsruta

visits.text: Two figures among the Begby carvings have names: Begbymannen, “the Begby Man,” and Danseren, “the Dancer.” These rock carvings, images cut into the rock, date from the early Bronze Age. You will also see an animal-shaped boat, carts, and suns. Begby is part of the Oldtidsruta, a series of signposted prehistoric sites along Route 110.

In the shade of the forest, a narrow trail leads to the Hornnes rock carvings. They depict 22 “solar boats,” carved in the early Bronze Age. At that time, the boat was the most important symbol. Wear closed-toe shoes: the trail can be wet.

The Solberg site is the easiest to view: it sits beside Route 110, with parking and interpretive signs. Its rock carvings depict four-wheeled carts, a large tree and a small one, and images of the sun. Some of the lines have been painted to make them easier to see. Avoid November through March: during the freezing season, most of the rock carvings along the Oldtidsruta are covered.

to_next_leg.road_type: E6

visits.text: From the top of Fredriksten’s walls, the view stretches across Halden, the fjord, and the lands of its former Swedish enemy. Construction of the fortress began in 1661, after the loss of the neighboring province of Bohuslän, ceded to Sweden in 1658. It withstood six attacks without ever being captured. Its walls cover about 20,000 m², and three separate forts protect it. The grounds remain open day and night, and admission is free.

On December 11, 1718, King Charles XII of Sweden was killed outside Fredriksten. Fredriksten Museum tells the story of his death and Halden’s military history, from the 1640s to 1905. It occupies the Østre kurtine, the eastern curtain wall: the long wall connecting two bastions. The exhibition “Det store fallet” (“The Great Fall”) covers everything from the king’s underwear to the monuments erected after his death. On the top floor, the former water tower offers panoramic views. The museum opens only during the warmer months: after mid-August, it is open only on weekends, from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m.

To save their town, the people of Halden burned it down. On July 4, 1716, Charles XII’s troops attacked at night. The residents then set fire to their own homes to keep the enemy from using them. The fortress held firm. Today, south of the pedestrian street, the Sørhalden neighborhood retains beautiful Empire-style houses, reflecting the neoclassicism of the early 19th century. Finish with a walk along the Tista, the river that runs through Halden.

If you have an extra morning in Halden, save it for Rød herregård, one of Norway’s best-preserved manor houses. Its garden, originally Baroque, was later expanded into an English landscape park. A curiosity lies hidden there. Ships delivering Norwegian timber to England returned loaded with English soil, used as ballast to stabilize them. Seeds in that soil gave rise to plants that still leave their mark on the garden. Guided tours of the house are available from May to September.

activities.text: Follow Karl XIIs sti, the Charles XII trail, from Halden’s market square to the fortress. The walk takes about 30 minutes. At each stop, the free Kulturpunkt app gives voice to a figure from the period, who describes their connection to the king. The trail ends at the Stevnesletta monument, erected in 1938 by Norway and Sweden near the spot where Charles XII fell. The king was standing in a trench about 170 m from the fortress. It is still uncertain who fired the shot.

practical_info.tip: Download the Kulturpunkt app before you leave: it guides you from one stop to the next and offers short challenges.

seo.h1_title: Østfold in 3 Days: Fredrikstad, Halden, and the Hvaler Islands
seo.intro_paragraph: This 3-day itinerary starts in Gamlebyen, Fredrikstad’s fortified old town, reached by ferry from the west bank of the Glomma River. It continues to the Hvaler Islands and Norway’s first marine national park, then follows the Oldtidsruta and its Bronze Age rock carvings to Halden. There, Fredriksten Fortress tells the story of the death of King Charles XII of Sweden in 1718.
seo.seo_hook: Gamlebyen and its free ferry, the Hvaler Islands coastal trail, Bronze Age rock carvings, and Halden’s fortress: Østfold in 3 days.
featured_list: Fredrikstad: Gamlebyen, a fortified town founded in 1567, and its free ferry
Hvaler: an 11.4 km coastal trail in Norway’s first marine national park
Oldtidsruta: Bronze Age rock carvings at Begby, Hornnes, and Solberg
Halden: Fredriksten Fortress, never captured despite six attacks
