itineraries.title: Telemark in 4 Days: Rjukan, Heddal, and the Telemark Canal
itineraries.subtitle: In 4 days, travel from Heddal Church, the Vemork plant, and Gaustatoppen to the locks of the Telemark Canal.
itineraries.notes: Rjukan’s Krossobanen cable car has been closed since June 2024, with reopening targeted for 2028. Travel from mid-June to mid-August, when canal boats, guided tours, and museums offer their most extensive operating schedules.
itineraries.climate: Aim for mid-June to mid-August, when attractions and boats are operating: average highs in Notodden are around 22 to 23 °C during this period, and August is the wettest month. At the summit of Gaustatoppen, at 1,883 m, it is much cooler: bring a warm jacket even in summer. Avoid winter: boats are docked, average highs fall below 0 °C in January, and Rjukan receives no direct sunlight from September to March.

visits.text: The most beautiful landmark of the trip comes at the very first stop: Heddal stavkirke, or Heddal Stave Church. “Stave” means its walls are supported by large vertical wooden posts rather than horizontal logs. It dates from the 13th century. Standing 29 m tall, it is the largest church of its kind in Norway. Inside, look for the 23 masks carved on the pillars. The adult ticket (110 NOK) includes a guided tour in English or Norwegian. The church is open from mid-May to mid-September. On Saturdays, weddings may interrupt visits.

Next, walk to Heddal Bygdetun, the village’s open-air museum, just a few steps from the church. It has around 15 historic buildings dating from the Middle Ages to the 1930s. In Rambergstugo, a former home, the walls feature decorations painted in 1784 by Olav Hanssen. The site is unstaffed, so you can wander freely among the houses. To see the interiors, ask the museum about guided tours available by reservation.

The world’s first calcium nitrate factory began operating in Notodden in 1905, producing fertilizer for farmland. The World Heritage Center, housed in a former industrial hall at the Tinfos industrial site, tells the story of this invention. The Birkeland–Eyde process heated air to several thousand degrees using an electric arc, a kind of continuous lightning bolt. Nitrogen from the air was then turned into a fertilizer sold as Norgessalpeter. The same ticket includes admission to Telemark Kunstmuseum, the art museum that shares the hall. From June 22 to August 9, both are open daily from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m.

Grønnbyen, literally “the green town,” is the workers’ housing district built by Hydro in the early 20th century. Its 25 duplex houses are divided vertically: each family had its own half, from the ground floor to the roof. Farther on, the Villamoen neighborhood has 17 villas built for engineers and managers in various styles, including Art Nouveau. At the far end stands Admini, the former home and office of Hydro founder Sam Eyde. It overlooks the factories and the lake. Hydro still uses it for meetings, so admire it from the street.

Despite its industrial roots, Notodden has become Norway’s blues town. Bok & Blueshuset, the “house of books and blues,” is its heart, housing a library, concert venues, and a tourist information office. The building rests on the concrete slab of Anlegg 5, a former industrial furnace hall. Founded in 1988, the Notodden Blues Festival attracts thousands of spectators each summer. The 2027 festival is scheduled for August 5 to 8: book your accommodations early if you plan to visit on those dates.

activities.text: Between large loading cranes and the waters of Lake Heddalsvatnet, Notodden’s industrial promenade follows the shoreline for 2 km. It begins near Hydroparken, Hydro’s former waterfront factories, where fertilizer production began. The path is flat and easy, suitable for all ages. Benches and lighting have been installed along the entire route, so the walk can also be taken in the evening after the museums close.

practical_info.tip: The promenade starts at Bok & Blueshuset (Storgata 1) and leads to the Nesøya campground.

visits.text: Vemork was the world’s largest power station when it opened in 1911. It houses Norsk Industriarbeidermuseum, the Norwegian Industrial Workers Museum. Its World Heritage Center explains the 2015 UNESCO designation. In Rjukan and Notodden, Norsk Hydro harnessed the power of waterfalls to make fertilizer from nitrogen in the air. The power stations, factories, railways, and workers’ housing districts are listed together. From late June to mid-September, the museum is open daily from noon to 6 p.m. Park at Vemork Bridge, then allow 20 minutes for the steep walk.

On the night of February 27–28, 1943, Norwegian commandos blew up Vemork’s heavy water cellar, in the basement of the hydrogen plant. Heavy water looks like ordinary water, but its hydrogen atoms are heavier. In a nuclear reactor, it slows the particles that sustain the chain reaction. Nazi Germany needed it for atomic research. The sabotage destroyed more than 500 kg of heavy water and halted production for several months. Rediscovered intact by archaeologists, the cellar has been open to visitors since 2022. Admission is included in the Vemork ticket.

Rjukan takes its name from a waterfall you will probably see almost dry: Rjukanfossen. Its largest drop measures 104 m. However, Norsk Hydro diverted its water to supply its power stations. The waterfall therefore only flows fully when the upstream Møsvatn reservoir has excess water. Water is also released for the Marispelet performance, held over four days in July. Park in the parking areas east of the Maristi Tunnel, upstream from Vemork. The trail around the mountainside opens up views of the gorge after about 250 m.

activities.text: Nothing tells Hydro’s story better than a walk through central Rjukan. The town was built almost from scratch in the 1910s and 1920s. Start at Torget, the market square. From September to March, the sun stays too low to rise above the surrounding mountains, including Gaustatoppen, leaving the town without any direct sunlight. Stop by Rjukan Church, consecrated in 1915. In 1965, a fire destroyed its interior during the filming of The Heroes of Telemark. It was consecrated again in 1968.

practical_info.tip: The tourist information office on Torget provides a map of the walk, which is marked with signs.

activities.text: Climb up to Solspeilet, Rjukan’s sun mirrors, installed in 2013 on the slope north of town, about 450 m above it. These three computer-controlled mirrors rotate to follow the sun. In winter, they reflect its light onto Torget, creating a patch of sunlight in the square. Hydro founder Sam Eyde proposed the idea back in 1913 but never brought it to life. The trail starts on the west side of town and runs about 1.7 km to the mirrors. It is steep, so bring sturdy shoes and water.

practical_info.tip: The mirrors are mainly used from September to March, when the square is in shadow; in summer, you can see them up close, without the patch of reflected sunlight.

to_next_leg.road_type: Fv651 mountain road
to_next_leg.justification: Gaustatoppen rises above the Rjukan valley, and road Fv651 climbs the mountainside in switchbacks: covering 16 km in 20 minutes is a true mountain drive, and the detour is no mistake.

visits.text: On a clear day, Gaustatoppen (1,883 m) offers views of nearly one-sixth of mainland Norway, an area of about 60,000 km². Gaustatoppen turisthytte, a staffed mountain lodge built in 1893 from stone from the mountain, serves drinks and simple meals from February to mid-October. From the lodge, allow about 20 minutes to walk over rocky terrain to the highest point. Even in July, bring a warm jacket and closed-toe shoes: at this elevation, it is considerably cooler than in Rjukan.

activities.text: Ascend Gaustatoppen through the mountain aboard Gaustabanen, the underground train. The first car travels horizontally through an 850 m tunnel. A second then climbs a very steep passage at a 39-degree incline to an elevation of 1,800 m. The Norwegian military and NATO had the tunnel excavated in the 1950s to provide year-round access to a military radio station at the summit. It has been open to the public since 2004. The ride takes about 15 minutes. Round-trip tickets cost 595 NOK per adult and 300 NOK for ages 5 to 15.

practical_info.tip: Depart from Svineroi on road Fv651, about 2 km from Gaustablikk. The train runs daily in summer; it closes for maintenance from late October to late November (October 26 to November 22 in 2026). Hikers can also climb from the Stavsro parking lot: 4.3 km with 700 m of elevation gain, taking about 2 hours each way, from June to September.

visits.text: According to legend, the statue of Saint Nicholas at Eidsborg stavkyrkje was immersed in a nearby pond every Midsummer Eve. This small medieval stave church stands in the hills above Dalen. Unusually, shingles—small wooden boards laid like tiles—cover both its walls and its roof. It is part of the Vest-Telemark Museum, an open-air museum that also preserves a wooden building dating to 1184. Admission: 150 NOK. The church opens only for guided tours at 11 a.m., 1 p.m., and 3 p.m., from mid-June to mid-August.

If you drop a banknote over the edge of Ravnejuvet, the “Raven’s Gorge,” it may float back up toward you, according to a story told in the valley. The explanation is simple: an updraft rises along the cliff face and pushes light objects upward. The cliff drops sheer for about 350 m to the Tokkeåi River. Access is via a narrow gravel road about 7 km long. Drive slowly, and approach the edge with caution.

activities.text: Start early to climb the 810 stone steps from Dalen to Rui, on the hillside above the village. Sherpas from Nepal built this staircase using local whetstone, a rock the region has exported for about a thousand years. Over 1 km, you gain 200 m in elevation, a climb of 20 to 30 minutes. The trail follows in the footsteps of two sisters from Rui, Ingerine and Gurine. Their life-size statues stand outside the Dalen tourist information office, which sells a book about their story.

practical_info.tip: The staircase starts near the ambulance station in central Dalen. It is accessible from April to October. Rui is private property: stay on the trail.

visits.text: With five chambers arranged like steps in a staircase, Vrangfoss is the largest lock station on the Telemark Canal. A lock is a chamber enclosed by gates: the water inside is raised or lowered to move a boat between different levels. Here, boats rise or descend 23 m. The name comes from the former waterfall, which was so “vrang,” meaning unruly, that logs floated down the river had trouble passing through it. Climb to the small yellow shelter by the upper chamber to watch the boats pass.

Ulefos Hovedgaard is a large manor house completed in 1807 in the Empire style, the neoclassical style of Napoleon’s era. It served as the summer residence of the Aall family, who lived there until 2007. The village is known for its ironworks, Ulefos Jernværk, founded in 1657. The reception rooms, including a “king’s room,” were designed to impress guests. Finish in the garden, which is very beautiful in summer. The manor is open in summer from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m., except Mondays: visit right after the cruise.

activities.text: The most beautiful way to see the Telemark Canal is from the deck of an old boat. This 105 km canal connects Skien to Dalen through 18 locks. Completed in 1892, it was considered in Europe to be the “eighth wonder of the world” at the time. The Ulefoss–Lunde–Ulefoss half-day trip begins with a bus ride to Lunde Lock. You then travel back down aboard the M/S Victoria or M/S Henrik Ibsen, passing through the Vrangfoss locks to Ulefoss. Meet at the Ulefoss locks bus stop at 12:05 p.m.; the boat arrives in Ulefoss at 3:20 p.m.

practical_info.tip: Book online no later than the day before: 755 to 925 NOK per adult, depending on the date. In 2026, the trip ran daily from May 19 to September 8. Both boats have an onboard restaurant.

activities.text: Head to Skien, a 30-minute drive from Ulefoss, for your fourth night. This is where the Telemark Canal begins: Skien Lock, the first of eight lock stations, raises boats just 5 m. Canal boats depart from the Hjellebrygga quay. The playwright Henrik Ibsen was born in this city. The next day, depart from Skien station, about 1 km from the center.

practical_info.tip: Skien station is the terminus for regional trains on the Vestfold Line, which run to Oslo.

seo.h1_title: Telemark in 4 Days: Rjukan, Heddal, and the Telemark Canal

Visit Vemork power station and its heavy water cellar, ride to the summit on a train through the mountain, and finish with a boat trip to Ulefoss.

itineraries.title: Røros in 3 Days: Copper Town, Mine, and Lake Femund
itineraries.subtitle: In 3 days, explore Røros, a UNESCO-listed copper town, Olav’s Mine, and Lake Femund by boat.
itineraries.notes: This itinerary is designed for summer: the Fæmund II boat sails only from mid-June to early September, and Olav’s Mine opens only on Thursdays and Saturdays from mid-September to late May. You can reach Røros by train or plane from Oslo, but getting to the mine and lake requires a car or the summer buses.
itineraries.climate: Aim for late June to mid-August: this is the season for boat trips and daily mine tours, with average highs around 18 °C in July. Bring a fleece and a windbreaker, as Røros sits at an elevation of 630 m. Avoid winter unless you are looking for extreme cold: average January lows hover around -14 °C, and the town holds southern Norway’s record low of -50.3 °C, set in 1914.

visits.text: The best starting point for understanding Røros is Smelthytta, the former copper smelter turned museum. From 1644 to 1977, the town depended on copper extracted from nearby mines. The ore, rock containing a small amount of metal, was first heated to drive off sulfur, then smelted here. These two stages consumed enormous quantities of wood. The current building, rebuilt in 1988, recreates the appearance of the 1888 smelter, which was destroyed by fire in 1953. The museum opens daily. Pick up the French audio guide, which is included in the ticket.

These dark hills on the edge of town are entirely human-made. Slegghaugan consists of slag heaps: the waste rock left after copper was smelted. Three centuries of smelting piled them up just steps from Smelthytta. They are now protected under Norway’s Cultural Heritage Act. Climb to the top for views across the town’s wooden rooftops and its whitewashed church.

Farmyards hide behind the wooden facades along Bergmannsgata, “Miners’ Street.” The street’s layout dates to the 17th century, shortly after the town was founded. A typical house also sheltered four to six cows: miners’ families partly supported themselves by raising livestock. UNESCO specifically recognizes this adaptation to a harsh, isolated life. Walk the street from end to end, then head to Kjerkgata, Røros’s other main street.

If you are wondering why Røros has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1980, Kjerkgata, “Church Street,” provides the answer. Swedish troops burned the town in 1678 and 1679. It was then rebuilt in wood. After the mining company went bankrupt in 1977, almost nothing was altered. Along this commercial street, each property combined a farm, a trading house, and living quarters. Follow it uphill toward the church that gave it its name.

It is nicknamed Bergstadens Ziir, “the ornament of the mining town.” Completed in 1784, Røros Church seats about 1,600 people, making it one of Norway’s largest churches. The mining company paid 23,000 riksdaler, the currency of the time, for it—equivalent to about 450 years of a miner’s wages. Inside, the altar is at the bottom, the pulpit above it, and the organ at the very top. The king had his own box above the entrance, while the poorest people sat in the galleries. In summer, the church opens Tuesday through Saturday, from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m.

Five degrees year-round: that is the temperature awaiting you in Olavsgruva, Olav’s Mine, 13 km from Røros. The guided tour lasts about 1 hour and takes you through two mines. Excavation at Nyberget began in 1650, while Olavsgruva operated from 1936 to 1972. You descend 50 m underground and walk 500 m to Bergmannshallen, the “Miners’ Hall.” Bring a warm jacket and sturdy shoes, as the ground is slippery. Admission costs 220 kroner per adult.

The surface buildings at Olavsgruva also tell the mine’s story. The headframe, built over the shaft in 1936, also helped ventilate the mine. The café occupies a house from Bergmannsgata in Røros that was moved here in 1947. Pay particular attention to the 1946 ore ropeway: this aerial cable, about 1.3 km long, carried ore. Norway’s Directorate for Cultural Heritage describes it as the only intact example of its kind remaining in the country. Allow half an hour for the small exhibition on the region’s geology.

activities.text: If you have an extra hour, walk around the Storwartz mining field, the area of former mines surrounding Olav’s Mine. Nine mines were opened here, the first in 1645. In 1646, the king of Denmark–Norway granted the company all rights to minerals, forests, and rivers within a circle with a radius of about 45 km. This circle is called the Circumference. It gives its name to the UNESCO-listed site, “Røros Mining Town and the Circumference.” Its center is near here. Stay away from the old mine shafts.

practical_info.tip: From mid-June to mid-August, a shuttle leaves Malmplassen square in Røros at 10:15 a.m. for the 11 a.m. tour and departs from the mine at 12:30 p.m.; at other times, you can only get here by car. In summer, the mine offers daily tours; from mid-September to late May, tours run only on Thursdays and Saturdays at 3 p.m. Book online through the Rørosmuseet website.

visits.text: Small, poor, yet famous: Sleggveien is one of Røros’s most modest streets. Its houses, built around 1840–1850 partly from salvaged materials, had neither barns nor cowsheds. Day laborers, poor widows, and single mothers lived here. It is also called “Pippi’s Street,” because an episode of Pippi Longstocking was filmed here. The street ends at the foot of Slegghaugan: climb the slag heaps to see it from above.

Day and night, the Røros smelter never stopped. Hytteklokka, the smelter bell, set the rhythm of this work: it rang at the end of each shift, when one crew of workers gave way to the next. Its current bell tower dates to the 1890s. The Hyttelva River, right beside it, explains the smelter’s location: the first one was built in 1646 near its waterfall. Look for the bell tower as you walk along the river near Smelthytta.

activities.text: You will gain a better understanding of Røros on the guided town tour organized by Rørosmuseet. It starts at Smelthytta, on Malmplassen square, and ends inside the church. Allow about 1 hour 20 minutes. From late June to mid-August, a Norwegian-language tour departs daily at 11 a.m., and an English-language tour at 1 p.m. Tickets cost 160 kroner per adult, and accompanied children under 16 enter free.

practical_info.tip: From June 1 to 19 and August 16 to September 10, there is one departure daily at 11 a.m.; from September 11 to late May, departures are on Thursdays and Saturdays at 11 a.m. Tickets are available on the Rørosmuseet website.

to_next_leg.road_type: Femundveien to the Synnervika dock

activities.text: The most scenic way to reach Femundsmarka is still aboard Fæmund II, a metal-hulled boat that has sailed Lake Femund since 1905. Too large to be transported in one piece, it arrived in sections at Synnervika, where it was assembled. Its boiler, the heart of the steam engine, was too large to be cut apart: six horses pulled it on a sled. Femund, Norway’s third-largest lake, stretches for 60 km at an elevation of 662 m. In summer, the boat leaves Synnervika daily at 9 a.m.

practical_info.tip: Day tickets start at 499 kroner. The boat sails from mid-June to early September: daily at the height of summer, and Friday through Sunday at the beginning and end of the season. Check the current year’s schedule at femund.no. If you do not have a car, bus 540 leaves Røros at 8:15 a.m. and arrives in Synnervika at 8:55 a.m.; parking at the dock is free. The boat also stops at Femundshytta, a copper smelter that operated from 1743 to 1822, built there to take advantage of the forests: its slag heaps are still visible behind the farm.

to_next_leg.road_type: Fæmund II boat from Synnervika to the Røa dock
to_next_leg.justification: Crossing Lake Femund on the Fæmund II, an actual scheduled service departing Synnervika at 9 a.m.; the distance is listed as 10 km, the straight-line distance between the two points, and the travel time of about 35 minutes remains an estimate, as no timetable for individual stops is published online.

visits.text: Røvollen is a self-service cabin with no warden, run by the Norwegian Trekking Association (DNT). It occupies a former summer pasture, a meadow where livestock were taken in summer. These meadows attracted unexpected visitors: musk oxen. A small herd from the Dovrefjell mountains settled in the area in 1971. The animals came here to graze. By 2021, only seven animals remained in the herd. If you encounter any, back away calmly and stay at least 200 m away.

Here, even dead trees are protected. Femundsmarka National Park, established in 1971, stretches between Lake Femund and the Swedish border. Its old, dead pines support rare species, including a lichen called ulvelav. The landscape of scattered pines, boulders, and lakes has changed little since the ice retreated about 10,000 years ago. The Sámi, the Indigenous people of northern Scandinavia, have herded their reindeer here since the 17th century. Campfires are prohibited from April 15 to September 15.

activities.text: Get off the Fæmund II at the Røa dock, in the busiest area of Femundsmarka National Park. A trail marked with the letter T leads to Røvollen cabin in an hour to an hour and a half. The cabin is near the Røa River, which flows down from Sweden to Lake Femund. Have a picnic there, then head back to the dock without lingering. The boat passes only once a day in each direction: note the return time on the timetable before getting off.

practical_info.tip: Dogs must be kept on a leash from April 1 to August 20. Røvollen cabin is closed from October 15 to February 15. After the boat returns to Synnervika, allow about 40 minutes to drive to Røros.

itineraries.title: Bergen in 2 Days: Bryggen, Fløyen, Ulriken, and Grieg
itineraries.subtitle: In 2 days, travel on foot and by light rail from Bergen’s old harbor to the summits of Fløyen and Ulriken.
itineraries.notes: Edvard Grieg’s villa at Troldhaugen is undergoing restoration until summer 2027: visits are limited to the grounds, the composer’s cabin, and his grave. The itinerary runs over a Saturday and Sunday because the KODE museum closes on Mondays and Tuesdays outside the summer season, and the Ulriken cable car closes on Mondays in the low season.
itineraries.climate: Best time to visit: May through August, with average highs of 15 to 20 °C. It rains on more than half the days of the year, and often in summer too: bring a waterproof jacket. If possible, avoid October through January, the wettest months, with more than 250 mm of rain per month and short days.

activities.text: The smell of the sea and the calls of fishmongers: Fisketorget, Bergen’s fish market, is a good place to start the day. Merchants and fishermen have gathered here since the 1200s. Since 2012, an indoor market hall, Mathallen, has brought together fishmongers and restaurants year-round. The outdoor stalls only open from May through the end of summer. Prices are high: ask for the price per kilogram before ordering.

practical_info.tip: Mathallen: Monday through Saturday, 9 a.m. to 9:30 p.m.; Sunday, 10 a.m. to 9:30 p.m. Outdoor market from May 1, 10 a.m. to 6 p.m.

visits.text: The best of Bryggen lies behind the facades: leave the waterfront and follow the narrow wooden passageways between the houses. This merchants’ quarter, designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1979, retains around 62 wooden buildings. Their current appearance dates from the rebuilding that followed the fire of 1702. From 1350 onward, the Hanseatic League, an alliance of Northern European trading cities, maintained its trading office here. From October through December, a guided tour of Schøtstuene and Bryggen in English takes place on Saturdays and Sundays at noon.

to_next_leg.road_type: Along the Bryggen waterfront
to_next_leg.justification: Walk between two nearby stops downtown; the route planner calculated a driving route (due to one-way streets, a detour, or a zero distance), while the indicated walk of 0.5 km in 7 minutes is correct.

visits.text: A 13th-century royal banquet hall nearly vanished in 1944: Håkonshallen, at the heart of Bergenhus Fortress. King Håkon Håkonsson had it built for his celebrations. In 1261, his son Magnus’s wedding brought 2,000 guests here. On April 20, 1944, a cargo ship loaded with explosives blew up in the nearby harbor. The blast damaged the hall, and its wooden roof burned. Following restoration, it reopened in 1961. Check the calendar: the hall is closed to visitors on days when official events take place.

Next, climb Rosenkrantz Tower (Rosenkrantztårnet), within the same fortress. Its oldest section is a royal tower from the 1270s. In the 1560s, Erik Rosenkrantz, the fortress governor, had Scottish stonemasons expand it. Each level served a purpose: dungeons at the bottom, the governor’s quarters above, and cannons at the very top. The tower opens daily at 10 a.m., except December 21–31. Adult admission: 170 Norwegian kroner; free for visitors under 18.

to_next_leg.justification: Walk between two nearby stops downtown; the route planner calculated a driving route (due to one-way streets, a detour, or a zero distance), while the indicated walk of 0.4 km in 6 minutes is correct.

visits.text: “Ást min, kyss mik,” meaning “my love, kiss me”: this medieval love note, carved in runes, is preserved at Bryggens Museum. Runes are the ancient alphabet of the Scandinavian peoples. The museum holds around 670 of these messages, most carved into pine wood and discovered in and around Bryggen since the fire of 1955. The museum building, dating from 1976, stands over the foundations of Bergen’s oldest houses, built in the first half of the 12th century. Open daily; free for visitors under 18.

to_next_leg.justification: Walk between two nearby stops downtown; the route planner calculated a driving route (due to one-way streets, a detour, or a zero distance), while the indicated walk of 0.1 km in 2 minutes is correct.

visits.text: Open flames were forbidden in Bryggen’s wooden houses for fear of fire. The merchants of the Hanseatic League therefore cooked and ate together at Schøtstuene, their assembly halls. Justice was also administered here. Bergen’s tourist office describes them as the last halls of their kind in the world. Beneath a glass floor, you can see the remains of a building dating from around 1280. Admission: 160 kroner. The neighboring St. Mary’s Church (Mariakirken), the city’s oldest building, generally opens only on certain weekdays, around noon.

to_next_leg.road_type: 7 minutes on foot, then the Fløibanen funicular

visits.text: The best panoramic view of Bergen is from the terrace on Fløyen, 320 m above sea level. You can take in the city, the fjord, and the surrounding mountains at a glance. The name Fløyen may come from a weather vane that once showed sailing ships the wind direction. In winter, night falls early, but the paths leading back down to the city are lit. The illuminated city can then be seen from afar. The summit restaurant, Fløirestauranten, opens daily.

activities.text: If you visit in summer, buy your Fløibanen ticket online or in the app: it costs less than at the ticket counter. This funicular, in service since 1918, climbs 302 m in about six minutes. Along its 848 m track, the incline reaches 26 degrees. The lower station is a five-minute walk from the fish market. You cannot reserve a departure time: when it is busy, departures run one after another.

practical_info.tip: Departures daily from 7:30 a.m. (8 a.m. on weekends) to midnight. Adult round-trip ticket: 145 kroner through December 31, 2026; 210 kroner online from April through September 2027.

activities.text: Then follow the path to Lake Skomakerdiket, about a ten-minute walk from Fløyen’s upper station. In summer, canoes are available to borrow for free. Goats also graze on the mountain during this season. With children, stop by Trollskogen, the “troll forest,” and the large playground. To get back down, allow about 45 minutes to walk to the city center, or take the funicular again.

practical_info.tip: The lakeside Skomakerstuen café opens on weekends and public holidays. In snowy or icy conditions, wear shoes with good traction.

to_next_leg.road_type: Fløibanen, Bybanen line 1 to Hop, 20 minutes on foot

visits.text: Edvard Grieg’s villa is under restoration until summer 2027, but the grounds of Troldhaugen remain open year-round. The Norwegian composer lived here from 1885 until his death in 1907. In 1891, he had a small cabin built beside Lake Nordåsvannet so he could compose away from visitors. Edvard and Nina Grieg’s tomb is carved into the rock face, overlooking the lake. From mid-May to mid-September, admission is charged Tuesday through Sunday. The 200-kroner ticket also includes admission to the KODE museums in the city center.

to_next_leg.road_type: 20 to 30 minutes on foot to Hop, then Bybanen line 1 to Byparken
to_next_leg.justification: Segment 1: 20 to 30 minutes on foot from Troldhaugen to the Hop stop; segment 2: Bybanen light rail, line 1, from Hop to Byparken, about 22 minutes; segment 3: a few minutes on foot to KODE; about 9 km in 50 minutes, with light rail covering most of the distance.

visits.text: Head straight to the Munch galleries at KODE, Bergen’s art museum. They are in the Rasmus Meyer building, beside the small lake in the city center. KODE describes its Edvard Munch collection as the third most important in the world. It includes Jealousy (1895) and Evening on Karl Johan Street (1892), named after Oslo’s main avenue. Save time for the Blumenthal Room, whose walls and ceiling were painted around 1760. Outside summer, the museum is closed on Mondays and Tuesdays; on weekends, it opens from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m.

to_next_leg.road_type: On foot via Torgallmenningen, Strandgaten
to_next_leg.justification: Trajet urbain fait à pied entre kode rasmus meyer et nordnesparken, environ 2200 m de marche réelle comptés 2 km : l'ancienne durée de 5 min venait du calcul voiture, elle est remplacée par 28 min de marche.

visits.text: Sea breezes, paths, and benches facing the fjord: Nordnesparken occupies the tip of the Nordnes peninsula, west of the city center. Look for the totem pole, a wooden pole carved in the style of the Indigenous peoples of North America’s Pacific Coast. Seattle, Bergen’s sister city, gave it in 1970 to mark the 900th anniversary of the city, traditionally said to have been founded in 1070. The more adventurous swim at Nordnes sjøbad, a heated seawater pool with a sauna, or directly in the sea.

to_next_leg.justification: A walk between two nearby stops in the city center; the route planner calculated a driving route (one-way streets, a detour, or zero distance), while the stated walk of 0.2 km in 3 minutes is correct.

visits.text: If you are traveling with children, set aside 1 hour 30 minutes for Akvariet i Bergen, the city’s aquarium. It opened in 1960 at the tip of the Nordnes peninsula. More than 300 species live here, from fish found along the Norwegian coast to crocodiles and snakes from tropical forests. The stars are still the penguins and sea lions, fed in front of visitors at scheduled times. The daily program, published on the aquarium’s website, lists feeding times. Adult admission: 380 kroner; a family ticket is available.

to_next_leg.road_type: On foot to the city center, Bybanen line 2 to Haukeland sjukehus, then uphill on foot to the cable car
to_next_leg.justification: Segment 1: about 20 minutes on foot from the aquarium to the city center; segment 2: Bybanen light rail, line 2, to Haukeland sjukehus, about 10 minutes; segment 3: a steep uphill walk to the Ulriken643 cable car, about 10 minutes, followed by a 5-minute cable car ride; about 7 km in 45 minutes.

visits.text: From the summit of Ulriken, at 643 m, you can take in all of Bergen at a glance. It is the highest of the seven mountains surrounding the city. The cable car even includes this elevation in its name: Ulriken643. At the summit, you will find a television tower, a restaurant, and a café. Strong hikers can walk to Fløyen along the Vidden route, a hike of about 5 hours across the mountains. From October through December, the cable car runs until 11 p.m. Thursday through Saturday: the nighttime view is worth the trip.

activities.text: Each cabin of the Ulriken643 cable car, upgraded in October 2021, holds fifty people. The ride to the summit takes about five minutes. To reach the lower station, take line 2 of Bybanen, Bergen’s light rail, to the Haukeland sjukehus stop, in front of Haukeland Hospital. Then walk uphill for 5 to 10 minutes along a steep street that can be icy in winter. From April through fall, a shuttle, Ulriksbussen, also leaves from the city center near the tourist information office.

practical_info.tip: October through December 2026: no departures on Mondays; 9 a.m. to 7 p.m. on Tuesdays, Wednesdays, and Sundays; 9 a.m. to 11 p.m. Thursday through Saturday. Adult round-trip ticket: 435 kroner.

seo.h1_title: Bergen in 2 Days: Bryggen, Fløyen, Ulriken, and Grieg
seo.intro_paragraph: This 2-day weekend can be enjoyed without a car, on foot and by funicular, tram, and cable car. The first day follows the harbor from the fish market to Bryggen’s wooden houses and Bergenhus Fortress, then heads up to Fløyen. The second takes you to Edvard Grieg’s park at Troldhaugen, the KODE museum, the Nordnes peninsula, and the summit of Ulriken.
seo.seo_hook: Bergen in 2 days without a car: Bryggen’s wooden houses, the Fløyen funicular, Munch at the KODE museum, Grieg’s park, and the Ulriken cable car.

Troldhaugen: Edvard Grieg’s composing cabin and lakeside grave

itineraries.title: Jostedalsbreen in 4 Days: Urnes, Fjærland, and Loen
itineraries.subtitle: In 4 days, travel from Urnes Stave Church to the glaciers of Nigardsbreen, Fjærland, Briksdal, and Loen.
itineraries.notes: Most sites are only open from May through September, including Urnes Church (May 2–September 30) and the Nigardsbreen boat service (June–September). For your departure from Loen, Sandane Airport in Anda is just over an hour’s drive away and has flights to Oslo operated by Widerøe.
itineraries.climate: Best time to visit: June through August, with average highs of 19–21 °C in Fjærland. Avoid fall and winter: from September through January, Fjærland receives more than 200 mm of rain per month, and most sites are only open from May through September. To walk on the ice, even in July, guides require warm, waterproof clothing that covers your entire body.

activities.text: You’ll land at Sogndal Airport (Haukåsen), served by Widerøe flights from Oslo and Bergen. Express boats also travel from Bergen up the Sognefjord to Sogndal. Continue the itinerary by car: follow road Fv55 for 17 km to Solvorn, on the Lustrafjord, the innermost arm of the Sognefjord. From there, a small ferry crosses to Ornes, the landing for Urnes Church. It holds only about ten cars, so cross on foot, as the church is just a short walk uphill from the landing.

practical_info.tip: The Solvorn–Ornes ferry runs every day, year-round. The crossing takes about 20 minutes.

to_next_leg.road_type: Fv55 to Solvorn, then a 20-minute ferry crossing

visits.text: The ferry crossing is worth the trip: Urnes Stave Church is the only church of its kind on the UNESCO World Heritage List, where it was inscribed in 1979. This type of church is supported by a framework of tall vertical posts. This one was built around 1130. Its north portal, carved around 1070 for an earlier church, was reused here. Its interlaced animals gave their name to the Urnes style, the last Viking decorative style. Open May 2–September 30, from 10:30 a.m. to 5:45 p.m., in groups of no more than 25: expect a wait.

activities.text: If the next tour group is full, wait your turn on the TRANQUIL trail. This poetry trail, opened in 2024, circles Urnes Church through the surrounding farmland and its apple orchards. Children can enjoy a playground, a nature trail, and a mock archaeological dig. At the neighboring Urnes Gard farm, a café sells local fruit, juices, and jams.

practical_info.tip: According to the 2026 schedule, the last ferry leaves Ornes at 6 p.m. daily. Check the schedule locally before lingering.

to_next_leg.road_type: 20-minute ferry crossing

visits.text: A small village today, Solvorn was once the market town for everyone living along the shores of Lake Hafslovatnet. The town also housed a courthouse. Its heyday came when the fjord served as the main highway. When road Fv55 was built higher up toward Hafslo, traffic bypassed Solvorn. Stroll from the landing, where a ferry has departed for Ornes since 1859, to the church built in 1883, just above the houses.

activities.text: You can rent a kayak in Solvorn and paddle on the Lustrafjord, across from Urnes Church. A guesthouse in the village rents single and double kayaks, with paddles and life jackets, for 500 NOK for 4 hours. It also rents bicycles for 400 NOK per day. On the water, keep your life jacket on, stay close to shore, and head back if the wind picks up.

practical_info.tip: The rental provider has only four single kayaks and one double: book the day before in summer.

to_next_leg.road_type: Via Hafslo and Gaupne, then through the Jostedalen valley

visits.text: Rebuilt in 2013 after the 2011 fire, the Breheimsenteret echoes the shapes of crevasses, the cracks in a glacier, and seracs, the blocks of ice that stand where it fractures. It is a visitor center for Jostedalsbreen National Park, home to the largest glacier in mainland Europe. The exhibition shows how ice shaped the valleys. A film follows the glacier through the seasons. The restaurant overlooks Nigardsbreen. In 2026, the center was open daily from May 1 through September 30, with hours of 9 a.m. to 7 p.m. in peak summer; admission was 125 NOK.

Jostedal Church, with its long white wooden nave, dates from around 1660. It replaced earlier churches on the same site, including a stave church probably dating from the 13th century. It is still the valley’s parish church. No visiting hours are published: if the door is closed, limit your visit to the exterior, in the center of Jostedal village.

activities.text: Beneath your feet, the ice of Nigardsbreen is a deep blue: the excursion is called Kort Blåistur, “short blue ice walk.” This glacier is an arm of Jostedalsbreen, a tongue of ice descending toward the valley. Between 1700 and 1748, during very cold winters, it advanced about 4 km and crushed farms. Guides from Jostedalen Breførarlag lead the excursion: 4 hours 30 minutes, including 1 hour 30 minutes on the ice, for ages 12 and up, with the boat ride and equipment included. In 2026, it ran daily from May 15 through September 25.

practical_info.tip: Book four or five days ahead in summer. With children ages 8 and up, choose the family excursion lasting 3 hours 30 minutes, including 45 minutes on the ice, offered in 2026 from July 6 through August 23. Never step onto the ice without a guide. You can still get close to the glacier: take the Brevegen toll road (90 NOK per car), then the lake boat, which runs from June through September and leaves you a 40-minute walk from the foot of the glacier.

to_next_leg.road_type: Via Gaupne, Sogndal, and the Frudal Tunnel

visits.text: Even in perfect weather, start at Norsk Bremuseum, the Norwegian Glacier Museum: it explains everything you will see afterward. The concrete and wood building was designed by Sverre Fehn, who won the Pritzker Prize, a major international architecture award, in 1997. You can handle ice taken from Supphellebreen, a nearby glacier. A film on a panoramic screen takes you into Jostedalsbreen National Park. The museum opens daily from April through October, with hours of 9 a.m. to 7 p.m. in June, July, and August; admission is 180 NOK.

Less than five minutes by car from the museum, a startling sight awaits: Bøyabreen, an arm of Jostedalsbreen, has melted so much in recent years that only remnants of ice remain. At its foot, the small lake Brevatnet collects meltwater. Waterfalls tumble down the cliffs at the head of the valley. Here you can see firsthand the glacial retreat the museum has just explained. Park in the nearest parking lot: a 200 m walk leads to the shore. A café and restaurant that opened in 1960 faces the glacier.

In Norwegian, it is called Bokbyen, “the book town.” In Fjærland, about 4 km of shelves filled with used books occupy the old buildings of the hamlet of Mundal. Browse the shelves in a former ferry waiting room, a barn, a bank, or a post office. Established in 1996, it was the first book town in the Nordic countries. The shops open daily from May through September, except on May 17, Norway’s national day.

The white wooden Fjærland Church has stood beside the fjord since 1861. It was once called Mundal Church, after the neighboring hamlet. In Norway, family names often come from the family’s original farm. This is how Walter Mondale, vice president of the United States from 1977 to 1981, got his name from this hamlet, where his paternal grandparents were born. The church is just steps from the bookstores: visit both on foot.

to_next_leg.road_type: Fjærland Tunnel, then Skei and Byrkjelo

visits.text: Completed in 1759, Old Olden Church (Gamle Olden kyrkje) has a Greek cross plan, with four equal arms. It is the only church with this layout in Nordfjord. It no longer serves as a parish church and operates as a small museum. It is only open to visitors in summer: check the posted hours before counting on a visit inside.

to_next_leg.road_type: Along Lake Oldevatnet

visits.text: Briksdalsbreen now ends on dry land, behind its small glacial lake. Yet this arm of Jostedalsbreen made headlines in the 1990s. Between 1967 and 1997, it advanced 465 m and covered the entire lake, while most of Europe’s glaciers were retreating. Since then, it too has been retreating: by 2007, it no longer reached the lake. Keep your distance from the glacier’s edge, as blocks of ice can break off without warning.

activities.text: You will walk about 3 km, with 200 m of elevation gain, from the bottom of the Briksdal valley to the lake at Briksdalsbreen. About a third of the way along, spray from Kleivafossen waterfall drenches the trail: keep a windbreaker handy. Allow 2 hours 30 minutes to 3 hours for the round-trip walk. The troll cars, small electric carts that run from May through October, reduce the walk to 700 m. Leave Loen early: many excursions from cruise ships calling at Olden come up here.

practical_info.tip: There is a parking fee at the trailhead.

visits.text: In 1905 and again in 1936, sections of Mount Ramnefjellet fell into Lake Lovatnet, which the road to Kjenndalsbreen follows. These rockfalls triggered giant waves, reaching up to 74 m in height in 1936. They leveled the hamlets of Bødal and Nesdal and killed 135 people in total. After a 17 km drive along the toll road from Loen, Kjenndalsbreen glacier is just a 15-minute walk from the parking lot. The road is closed in winter; the Kjenndalstova café opens from May through September.

activities.text: The fjord drops rapidly away beneath the Loen Skylift cabin: in about 5 minutes, it climbs 1,011 m, on a slope that reaches 60° in places. At the top, on Mount Hoven, the Skredfjellet trail (2 km one way, with 155 m of elevation gain) follows a gravel path suitable for all ages. In 2027, the cable car will run daily from May 1 through October 3, until 11 p.m. in July. Your ticket has no set return time: simply head back down before closing.

practical_info.tip: In the off-season, the cable car generally only opens Thursday through Sunday, and it shuts down for maintenance from November 30 through December 9, 2026. To have lunch at the summit restaurant, reserve a table in advance.

seo.h1_title: Jostedalsbreen in 4 Days: Urnes, Fjærland, and Loen
seo.intro_paragraph: This 4-day itinerary connects the valleys descending from Jostedalsbreen, the largest glacier in continental Europe, between the Sognefjord and the Nordfjord. You cross the Lustrafjord by ferry to the Urnes stave church, then walk on the ice of Nigardsbreen with a guide. At the museum in Fjærland, you learn why glaciers are retreating, before finishing in Loen, where a cable car climbs to 1,011 m above the fjord.
seo.seo_hook: Jostedalsbreen in 4 days: UNESCO-listed Urnes Church, the ice of Nigardsbreen, Fjærland’s glacier museum, Briksdal, and the Loen cable car.
featured_list: Urnes: the only stave church on the UNESCO World Heritage List
Nigardsbreen: a guided walk lasting 4 hours 30 minutes, including 1 hour 30 minutes on the ice
Fjærland: Sverre Fehn’s glacier museum and 4 km of bookshelves
Briksdalsbreen: a 3 km trail through the spray of Kleivafossen
Loen Skylift: a 1,011 m ascent in about 5 minutes

itineraries.title: Southern Hardanger in 3 Days: Trolltunga, Folgefonna, Rosendal
itineraries.subtitle: In 3 days, hike to Trolltunga and Buarbreen Glacier, then head to the Barony of Rosendal.
itineraries.notes: The Trolltunga hike takes a full day and can only be done without a guide from June 1 to September 30, by experienced hikers. Guided tours of the manor house at the Barony of Rosendal run from May 1 to August 30, 2026; after that, only groups are admitted, by request.
itineraries.climate: Best time to visit: mid-June through late August, with average highs of 17 to 18 °C in Odda. The Trolltunga plateau is much colder, and snow often covers the trail into June: bring warm clothing even in summer. Avoid October: rainfall becomes heavy, and from October through May, the Trolltunga hike requires a guide.

visits.text: An industrial town at the foot of a glacier, Odda actually got its start in tourism: in the early 20th century, more than 80 cruise ships called here each season. Then electricity generated by the rushing streams attracted industry. From 1908 to the early 2000s, the Smelteverket plant (“the smelter”) produced carbide, a chemical substance partly processed into fertilizer. In 2009, Norway nominated this industrial heritage for UNESCO World Heritage status. The tourist office, at the bus station, is open weekdays from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m.

In 1848, Lake Sandvinvatnet, south of Odda, partly inspired the setting of a famous Norwegian painting, “Bridal Procession on the Hardangerfjord.” It depicts a wedding procession crossing a fjord in rowboats. Adolph Tidemand painted the figures. Hans Gude painted the landscape, combining several places he had seen. Rv13 follows the lake’s eastern shore: pull into a turnout to look across at the valley rising toward Buarbreen Glacier.

to_next_leg.road_type: Rv13 along Lake Sandvinvatnet

visits.text: The roar drowns out everything as soon as you open the car door: Låtefossen plunges right beside Rv13. It is a twin waterfall. Two torrents descend from Lake Lotevatnet and merge halfway down. The water then passes beneath an old stone bridge with six arches, after a total drop of 165 m. Visitors have been coming to see it since the 19th century: the first tourists arrived from Odda in horse-drawn carriages. The parking lot is free but small, and the bridge is narrow: in summer, arrive early to avoid traffic jams.

activities.text: You can see Låtefossen from above by taking the old stone-surfaced road that starts 50 to 60 m south of the bridge. It climbs the eastern slope to a viewpoint above the falls. The ruins of a former café with panoramic views remain at the top. Låtefossen is not the area’s only waterfall: the Odda valley is sometimes called “the valley of waterfalls.” Cross Rv13 carefully to reach the start of the trail, as the tourist office advises.

practical_info.tip: The site is accessible year-round and free to visit. During busy summer periods, park only in designated spaces and follow local signs.

activities.text: For a chance to get near a glacier without a guide, Buarbreen makes a rewarding half-day outing from Odda. This outlet of the vast Folgefonna Glacier descends into the Buer valley, which you can reach by car, about 8 km from town. The marked trail is moderately difficult and runs 3 km each way, with about 600 m of elevation gain: allow 4 hours round-trip. It follows the river and crosses it on footbridges. Fixed ropes help you climb in places, and the final section is steep. Wear proper hiking boots.

practical_info.tip: Parking at Buer farm, at the end of the road: 185 NOK (Norwegian kroner). Usual season: late May through October. The glacier is constantly moving: the tourist office asks visitors to keep their distance. A guided glacier walk can be booked through the Odda tourist office.

visits.text: Norwegians call it Trolltunga, the “troll’s tongue”: a blade of rock jutting out over a sheer drop, about 700 m above Lake Ringedalsvatnet. It dates from the last ice age, about 10,000 years ago. Meltwater froze in cracks in the gneiss, a very ancient rock, breaking off blocks that the glacier carried away. Trolltunga is the part that stayed in place. Fewer than 800 hikers came each year before 2010, compared with more than 80,000 in 2016. In summer, expect to wait in line for a photo on the rock.

activities.text: Set aside a full day for the Trolltunga hike. From the P2 parking lot at Skjeggedal, at an elevation of 415 m, the round-trip hike is 27 km and takes 8 to 12 hours. Adding up all the uphill sections, you will climb about 1,200 m. The P3 parking lot at Mågelitopp, at 860 m, reduces the round trip to 20 km and 7 to 10 hours. You can hike without a guide from June 1 to September 30, and only if you have mountain hiking experience. Start early: the Skjeggedal road is only open from 6 a.m. to 9 p.m.

practical_info.tip: 2026 parking rates: P1 Tyssedal, 330 NOK per day (38 km round-trip, about 15 hours); P2 Skjeggedal, 550 NOK including the toll; P3 Mågelitopp, 600 NOK plus a 220 NOK toll, with 30 spaces that must be reserved at trolltunganorway.com/parking, open June 8 to September 30 with entry before 11 a.m. Shuttle buses run from Odda to Skjeggedal from mid-May through late September, with the first departure at 5:45 a.m., followed by a bus connection from Skjeggedal to Mågelitopp. From October through May, go only with a guide.

to_next_leg.road_type: Skjeggedal road, open from 6 a.m. to 9 p.m.
to_next_leg.justification: The starting point is the Trolltunga rock, at the end of the hike included in this stage: the drive only starts at the parking lot, then follows the narrow Skjeggedal road downhill through hairpin turns; 19 km in 40 minutes, or about 28 km/h, remains plausible—the routing engine misplaced the starting point.

visits.text: The Tysso I power plant, on the fjord in Tyssedal, houses Kraftmuseet, a museum of hydroelectric power and industry. From 1908 to 1989, it supplied electricity to Odda’s factories. Water flowed down through pipes from 400 m above, creating very high pressure. It was the first power plant of this type in Northern Europe. Don’t miss the control room with its marble panels. The museum is open daily from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. from May 23 to August 30; admission is 125 NOK.

activities.text: Next, climb to Lilletopp, at the top of the penstock, the large pipes that carried water down from the mountain to the power plant. The trail, equipped with steps and handrails, is 3.3 km round-trip with about 250 m of elevation gain: allow 40 to 50 minutes to reach the top. Up there, you can see where the old water tunnels ended, with views across to the Sørfjord, an arm of the Hardangerfjord, and Folgefonna Glacier. Park at P1, near the Tyssohallen sports hall: your museum ticket includes 3 hours of free parking there.

practical_info.tip: The trail is accessible from February to November and suitable for children. In summer, guided tours leave the museum at set times.

to_next_leg.road_type: Folgefonna Tunnel, 11 km beneath the glacier

visits.text: Turquoise water with a strip of ice at the far end: this is Lake Bondhusvatnet, at the foot of Bondhusbreen Glacier. Its color comes from glacial flour, a very fine rock dust ground down by the glacier. It floats in the water and mainly reflects blue and green light. Over the past century, the glacier has retreated considerably and is now visible only at the end of the valley. It was in this valley that Queen Sonja of Norway officially opened Folgefonna National Park on May 14, 2005. Picnic tables await by the water.

If you follow the Maurangsfjord along the Fv551 near Sundal, Furebergsfossen waterfall flows beneath the road. After a free fall of 20 m, the water flows straight into this arm of the Hardangerfjord. You can get very close, and a rainbow often forms in the spray. Do not stop on the roadway: the road is narrow and hugs the cliff, so park in the small parking lot nearby.

activities.text: In 1863, shipowner Johan Martin Dahll had the Isvegen, the “ice road,” built to sell ice from Bondhusbreen Glacier. Blocks weighing about 18 kg crossed the lake by rowboat, then traveled down to the dock by cart. They were used to keep food cool before the invention of the refrigerator. Much of the ice melted during the journey, and the trade ended after a few shipments. Today, this 2.3 km gravel path leads to Lake Bondhusvatnet on foot: allow 2 hours round-trip for this easy walk.

practical_info.tip: Parking: 125 NOK per day, 500 m from the Fv551 (follow signs for “Bondhusbrea”). In summer 2026, police closed the far end of the valley near the glacier until September 1 because of a risk of flash flooding. Follow the signs on site: if access is closed, turn back at the lake. Swimming is prohibited because the lake supplies drinking water to Bondhus and Sundal.

visits.text: The Barony of Rosendal (Baroniet Rosendal) alone makes this stop worthwhile. It is the only barony Norway has ever had. Ludvig Rosenkrantz built this manor house between 1661 and 1665. In 1678, King Christian V, who ruled Denmark and Norway, attached a baronial title to the estate. In 1927, the last owner donated it to the University of Oslo. Guided tours of the manor house: from June 22 to August 9, 2026, tours depart daily from 11 a.m. to 6 p.m., with less frequent departures in May, June, and late August. Garden and manor house ticket: 210 NOK.

The scent of roses lingers into fall: in Rosendal Have, the Barony’s garden, around 2,000 rosebushes bloom from June to November. The Renaissance garden and its rose beds are about 300 years old. Around them, a Romantic landscape park was laid out around 1850, with a stone tower beside a pond. The garden remains open year-round, with garden-only admission costing 150 NOK. Take a break in the old kitchen (Gamlakjøkenet), which serves lappar, small Norwegian pancakes, with coffee.

Kvinnherad Church (Kvinnherad kyrkje) is a white stone church built in the mid-13th century in the heart of Rosendal. In 1678, it became part of the new barony’s estate. Many members of the Rosenkrantz family, the lords of the manor, are buried here. In season, guided tours of the church are available: ask at the Barony’s reception desk for times.

An outdoor geology museum or a playground? Rosendal’s Steinparken, the “stone park,” is a bit of both. Sculptor Bård Breivik and stonemason Rolf Karlsen shaped large blocks here amid a collection of rocks from the region. Waterwheels and pools where children can sail small boats keep them entertained. The park also tells the story of life on Earth and fossils. Admission is free year-round; the Dinosaur House (Dinosaurhuset) has its own opening hours.

If it rains in Rosendal, head to the Folgefonnsenteret on the dock: this exhibition center is devoted to Folgefonna National Park. Its galleries follow the journey of water from the glacier to the fjord. They also show how a warming climate is changing these landscapes. Four nature films round out the visit, including one about life beneath the surface of the fjord. Admission is 125 NOK. The tourist office, in the same building, is open daily from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. through August 31.

seo.h1_title: Southern Hardanger in 3 Days: Trolltunga, Folgefonna, Rosendal
seo.intro_paragraph: This 3-day itinerary explores Southern Hardanger, from Odda to Rosendal. First, you hike to Buarbreen Glacier, then devote a full day to the Trolltunga hike. After the Tyssedal power plant museum, the tunnel beneath Folgefonna Glacier takes you to Lake Bondhusvatnet, then to the gardens of the Barony of Rosendal.
seo.seo_hook: Trolltunga, Buarbreen Glacier, Låtefossen waterfall, and the Barony of Rosendal: 3 days of hiking and heritage in Southern Hardanger.
featured_list: Odda: a former factory town at the head of the Sørfjord
Låtefossen: two waterfalls that merge before flowing beneath the road
Buarbreen: 4 hours round-trip to the glacier terminus
Trolltunga: 20 to 27 km round-trip for a full day of hiking
Tyssedal: the Tysso I power plant and the climb to Lilletopp
Bondhusvatnet: the old ice road to the turquoise lake
Rosendal: a manor house from 1665, a rose garden, and a 13th-century church
